Argument:
Harper Bank should prevail because Mary Winston’s testamentary plan satisfies § 2055(e)(3) and the underlying policy of the charitable deduction.

First, the governing “date of execution” is 1971. Section 2055(e)(3)(C)(iii) looks to when the “governing instrument was executed.” In ordinary testamentary usage, “execution” means the original signing with required formalities. Congress knew how to tie codicils to execution and affirmatively removed such linkage in the statute; the Court should not reinsert it. Traditional probate doctrines of “republication by codicil” serve state-law purposes (e.g., incorporating later facts), but § 2055(e)(3) is a federal tax provision aimed at encouraging post‑mortem correction of pre‑change instruments. Treating the 1982 codicil as a new execution would frustrate that remedial purpose for no tax‑policy reason, especially where Winston’s basic plan—a life interest for Fletcher, remainder to Elmwood—never changed.

Second, the pre‑reformation remainder was sufficiently “presently ascertainable,” and any residual concern is cured by the state‑court reformation, which § 2055(e)(3) expressly validates. The trust’s payments for Fletcher’s expenses are tethered to objective, real‑world limits: medical expenses actually incurred; taxes calculated under established rules; and “upkeep and improvements” reasonably necessary to maintain a single Riverside residence. As in Ithaca Trust, the standard is not metaphysical certainty but whether, at death, actuarial methods can value the charitable remainder based on reasonable expectations. An octogenarian life tenant with defined categories of support expenses, tied to one residence, yields a determinable remainder—far removed from unfettered invasion of principal for undefined “happiness” or “benefit.”

Finally, the 1988 reformation lawfully converted Fletcher’s interest into a fixed annuity, bringing the trust into technical compliance while preserving Winston’s charitable intent. Section 2055(e)(3) exists precisely to salvage such charitable remainders. Denying the deduction would elevate formalism over Congress’s remedial design and Winston’s clear donative purpose to Elmwood University.

Section 1382(c)(2)(A) creates a deliberate carve‑out from Retrospective Monthly Accounting for the first (and optional second) month of eligibility: benefits “shall be computed on the basis of income… and other relevant circumstances in such month.” That text requires a fresh, month-specific assessment, not mechanical carry‑forward of earlier income. The nonrecurring character of a “gate release” payment is precisely such a “relevant circumstance”: by its nature it is not available to meet ongoing subsistence needs.

The Secretary’s policy nullifies this statutory protection. By treating the same one-time payment as if it were recurring income for three months, the agency converts an express hardship-avoidance provision into an engine of hardship. Congress adopted § 1382(c)(2)(A) so that initial benefits would reflect actual need in those fragile months, not be depressed by prior or nonrecurring resources.

Section 1382(c)(5) reinforces that reading. There, Congress singled out certain one-time payments and decreed they be counted only once, confirming a general principle: nonrecurring income is to be aligned with the period in which it is actually available. The Secretary inverts that structure. Under basic canons, specific provisions aimed at first-month hardship and one-time payments control over general RMA mechanics. The statute nowhere authorizes “triple counting” a single nonrecurring payment.

Nor can administrative convenience override Congress’s command. RMA is permissible only to the extent it is applied consistently with § 1382(c)(2)(A)’s requirement to account for “other relevant circumstances” in the initial months. Here, the agency has read that phrase out of the statute.

Because the Secretary’s policy disregards the text, structure, and remedial purpose of §§ 1382(c)(2)(A) and (5), it is unlawful. The Carter Class is entitled to relief and to recalculation of benefits without multi‑month deductions for a single gate‑release payment.

Section 1382(c)(2)(A) creates a deliberate break from ordinary RMA in the first (and optionally second) month of (re)eligibility: benefits “shall be determined for such month on the basis of the income of such individual … and other relevant circumstances in such month.” That text is both mandatory (“shall”) and holistic: the agency must consider not just the dollar amount received, but circumstances bearing on how that income should affect subsistence in those initial months.

For Carter Class members, the quintessential “relevant circumstance” is that the gate-release payment is nonrecurring and already spent on basic survival before SSI resumes. Treating that one‑time, pre‑eligibility payment as if it were continuing income—so that it depresses benefits in month one prospectively and then again via the RMA look‑back in months two and three—ignores that statutory command and produces exactly the hardship Congress sought to avoid.

Section 1382(c)(5) confirms the point. Congress expressly barred multiple‑month counting of specified nonrecurring payments in the RMA system. That provision is remedial and illustrative, not exhaustive: it shows Congress’s judgment that repeating the impact of singular income is incompatible with the program’s subsistence purpose. It would be perverse to read § 1382(c)(5) as a license to triple‑count every other one‑time payment, especially in the very months Congress carved out for individualized, circumstance‑based calculation.

Nor can administrative convenience override the statute’s text and purpose. The Secretary’s guidance effectively erases the transitional protection of § 1382(c)(2)(A) by ensuring that the same gate‑release payment suppresses benefits three times. That approach is arbitrary and contrary to law: it treats “retrospective” accounting as a rigid formula, rather than a default subject to explicit statutory exceptions.

Properly construed, §§ 1382(c)(2)(A) and 1382(c)(5) bar multi‑month reduction based on a single, nonrecurring gate‑release payment. Judgment should be entered for the Carter Class.

Section 1382(c)(2)(A) squarely directs that the benefit for the first (and, at the Secretary’s option, second) month “shall be determined on the basis of the income of such individual … and other relevant circumstances in such month.” For Andrew Carter and the Carter Class, the most salient “relevant circumstance” is that the gate-release payment is nonrecurring, tied uniquely to the moment of discharge. Once that month passes, the factual predicate for treating that money as available monthly income disappears.

The Secretary’s policy disregards this statutory command by mechanically treating a single, past, nonrecurring payment as if it were continuing income, thereby depressing benefits in up to three months. That transforms the protective “transitional computation cycle” into a punitive triple deduction, precisely the hardship Congress sought to avoid when it required a fresh, circumstance-sensitive calculation for the first month(s) of eligibility.

Section 1382(c)(5) reinforces this reading. Congress there recognized that some payments are so atypical that counting them month after month would be inequitable, and therefore required them to be charged off once. The Secretary inverts that protection: unless Congress has itemized a payment in (c)(5), the agency claims license to spread its effect across multiple months—even when, as here, it is plainly nonrecurring and tied to reentry from detention.

That approach violates basic canons of interpretation. The specific protection in (c)(2)(A) for the initial month(s), keyed to “other relevant circumstances,” cannot be nullified by a general administrative interest in convenience. Nor may the agency construe the enumeration in (c)(5) to negate the broader, textually mandated inquiry into actual circumstances in the first month.

Properly read, §§ 1382(c)(2)(A) and (c)(5) require that a one-time, nonrecurring gate-release payment affect benefits only once, not repeatedly. The Carter Class should prevail.

Section 1382(c)(2)(A) squarely rejects the Secretary’s “triple deduction” practice. For the first month of eligibility (and, at the Secretary’s option, the second), Congress commanded that the benefit “shall be payable… on the basis of income… and other relevant circumstances in such month.” A core “relevant circumstance” is whether income is nonrecurring. A one-time gate-release payment, given to smooth reentry, is fundamentally different from ongoing wages. Treating it as if it recurs—by allowing it to depress three months of benefits—ignores the statutory requirement to account for the actual circumstances of that month.

Congress adopted RMA to promote administrative efficiency, but also expressly carved out the first (and possibly second) month to prevent hardship. If the Secretary may nonetheless use the same nonrecurring payment to reduce multiple months, that carve-out is meaningless: Congress’s protection for newly eligible individuals would be nullified precisely when need is greatest.

Section 1382(c)(5) confirms this reading. There Congress singled out certain lump-sum payments that, even under RMA, “shall be taken into account only for such month.” That provision embodies a broader principle: nonrecurring sums should not repeatedly erode subsistence-level benefits. It would be anomalous to treat specially protected one-time payments more favorably than equally nonrecurring gate-release funds that serve an identical transitional function.

The Secretary inverts the canon of expressio unius. The specific list in § 1382(c)(5) operates within the RMA regime; it does not authorize disregard of “other relevant circumstances” in § 1382(c)(2)(A)’s separate, hardship-preventing regime for initial months. Where Congress spoke twice, the provisions must be harmonized: first-month calculations must reflect the nonrecurring nature of income, and RMA may not be applied in a way that recreates the very hardship Congress sought to avoid.

Accordingly, the gate-release payment can be counted, at most, once. The Carter Class should prevail.

Section 1382(c)(2)(A) carves out a specific protection from the usual Retrospective Monthly Accounting regime: for the first (and optionally second) month of eligibility, benefits must be computed based on “income … and other relevant circumstances in such month.” That directive displaces the normal look‑back and requires a fresh, month‑specific assessment. A quintessential “relevant circumstance” is that income is nonrecurring. Treating a one‑time gate payment as though it were a stream of income continuing over three months ignores that fact and violates the statutory command to account for the actual circumstances of the first month.

The Secretary’s approach effectively re-imports the look‑back method into the very months Congress singled out for special, hardship‑preventing treatment. It allows the same dollar to suppress subsistence benefits up to three times, turning a protective exception into a penalty.

Section 1382(c)(5) reinforces this reading. Congress there expressly recognized that some payments are nonrecurring and must therefore be “counted only for the month in which received.” That provision is not an exhaustive list of all nonrecurring income; it is a concrete instantiation of a broader principle already built into § 1382(c)(2)(A): when Congress departs from RMA to focus on “income … and other relevant circumstances” in the initial month, it means to prevent prior or singular resources from cascading through multiple months of reduced benefits.

The Secretary’s expressio unius argument fails because it treats § 1382(c)(5) in isolation and nullifies the operative “relevant circumstances” language in § 1382(c)(2)(A). At minimum, the statute is ambiguous. Under familiar canons, ambiguities in social‑welfare statutes must be resolved in favor of beneficiaries and in a manner that advances the core purpose of ensuring a minimum level of subsistence. The Carter Class’s interpretation does exactly that; the Secretary’s triple‑deduction regime does not.

The statutory text and structure support the Secretary’s interpretation.

First, § 1382(c)(2)(A) requires that the Secretary compute benefits for the first (and at the Secretary’s option, second) month based on the individual’s “income … and other relevant circumstances in such month.” Nothing in this phrase bars later months from reflecting that same income under RMA. It simply instructs how to compute the first-month amount—prospectively, taking account of the actual income in that month. The Secretary’s policy does exactly that.

Second, § 1382(c)(5) confirms that Congress knew how to limit the effect of one-time payments to a single month and chose to do so only for specified categories. By negative implication, unlisted one-time income—like a gate-release payment—remains subject to the ordinary RMA rules, even if its economic impact is felt across multiple months. Reading § 1382(c)(2)(A) to create a broad, unstated, one-month-only rule for all nonrecurring income would render § 1382(c)(5)’s specific carveouts largely superfluous.

Third, the Carter Class’s “triple deduction” framing misunderstands RMA’s temporal logic. The payment is counted once as actual income in the first month under the transitional rules and then once again when that same month’s income is looked back to in the third month. That is not forbidden double counting; it is precisely how RMA is designed to function for all income.

Finally, RMA is a congressionally endorsed system aimed at administrative feasibility, accuracy, and prevention of overpayment. The Secretary’s detailed guidance reasonably implements that scheme and fits comfortably within the statutory text. At minimum, any ambiguity should be resolved in favor of the agency’s longstanding, reasonable interpretation.

The statutory text and structure confirm that the Secretary’s treatment of Carter’s gate-release payment is lawful.

First, § 1382(c)(2)(A) creates a limited, transitional departure from Retrospective Monthly Accounting (RMA) for the first (and optionally second) month of eligibility: the benefit “shall be based on the income … and other relevant circumstances in such month.” Nothing in that language bars the later operation of the ordinary RMA regime on the same income once it has actually been received. “Relevant circumstances” ensures accurate, month‑specific initial calculations; it does not create an implied, across‑the‑board rule that all nonrecurring income may be counted only once.

Second, § 1382(c)(5) expressly lists particular payment types that “shall be taken into account only for such month.” Under the familiar canon expressio unius est exclusio alterius, Congress’s choice to single out specific one‑time payments for one‑month‑only treatment indicates that other nonrecurring income remains fully subject to the standard RMA rules, including multi‑month effects. If Congress had intended a general prohibition on multiple‑month impact for all nonrecurring income received early in eligibility, it knew how to say so and did not.

Third, the Secretary’s interpretation fits the statute’s evident administrative and anti‑fraud purposes. RMA exists “to bring predictability and correctness” to benefit calculations by tying them to verified, past income and by minimizing overpayments. Applying Carter’s gate‑release income prospectively in month one and then through the RMA look‑back in later months is a straightforward application of that system, not a forbidden “triple deduction.”

Finally, the challenged policy appears in detailed, contemporaneous guidance implementing a complex scheme. At minimum, any ambiguity in how §§ 1382(c)(2)(A) and (c)(5) interact should be resolved under Chevron in favor of the Secretary’s reasonable, administrable construction.

The statutory text and structure confirm that the Secretary’s method is lawful and reasonable.

First, § 1382(c)(2)(A) requires that the first (and optional second) month be computed based on “income … and other relevant circumstances.” Nothing in that language directs that nonrecurring income be counted only once, or insulated from later months under RMA. “Relevant circumstances” is a broad, administrative instruction; it does not silently carve out a categorical exception to the retrospective system Congress elsewhere designed in detail.

Second, Congress spoke directly to when income may be counted only once in § 1382(c)(5), expressly identifying specific types of payments that are limited to a single month’s deduction. Under basic interpretive principles, the express inclusion of specified one‑month‑only items implies the exclusion of others. If Congress had intended all nonrecurring income in an initial eligibility month to be single‑month income, it would not have needed the carefully enumerated list in § 1382(c)(5).

Third, the Secretary’s transitional computation rules faithfully implement the statutory RMA framework. For the first and second months, the agency prospectively accounts for the individual’s actual circumstances, including the gate‑release payment. By the third month, the statute itself requires a return to the standard two‑month look‑back. First, the Part-time Workers Regulations must be interpreted consistently with Framework Agreement Directive 97/81, which uses the phrase “solely because” of part‑time status. Parliament implemented the Directive knowing that language and without creating a broader, freestanding concept of part‑time discrimination. The Regulations’ phrase “on the ground that” must therefore be read as importing the Directive’s negotiated limitation: protection against treatment where part‑time status is the single operative cause, not merely one factor among many. To reinterpret that wording as “one effective reason” would expand domestic law beyond the EU instrument it implements, in conflict with the principle of conforming interpretation and the clear policy balance struck to avoid disproportionate burdens on employers.

Second, even if a looser causation standard applied, Reeves’s claim still fails. The circuit fee is a flat, role-based charge applied identically to every driver, full-time and part-time, and is justified by a neutral, sector‑standard business objective: funding the booking platform in lieu of taking a commission on fares. The fee structure does not distinguish by hours worked and does not turn on part‑time status at all; any heavier impact on part‑timers arises only from their personal choice to work fewer hours and earn less, not from differential treatment by Stone Rides.

Third, Reeves is not in a like-for-like position with full‑time drivers in economic terms: they generate more income and thus absorb fixed costs differently. That difference relates to volume of work, not to contractual status.

Accordingly, the adverse impact alleged is neither treatment “solely because” of part‑time status nor, in substance, treatment “on the ground” of such status. The claim should be dismissed.

Stone Rides Inc should prevail because Reeves has not shown that his part‑time status was the sole cause of any less favourable treatment, which is the proper standard under the 2000 Regulations when read consistently with Directive 97/81.

First, the governing EU Framework Agreement uses the phrase “shall not be treated in a less favourable manner than comparable full‑time workers solely because they work part time.” That language is clear and deliberately restrictive. The UK Regulations must, so far as possible, be interpreted consistently with that text and the negotiated balance it reflects. Reading “on the ground that” as encompassing any contributing factor would impermissibly expand protection beyond what the Directive authorises, effectively rewriting “solely because” out of existence.

Second, the impugned “circuit fee” is facially neutral and applies identically to all drivers, whatever their hours. The undisputed principal reason for the fee is a legitimate business one: to generate revenue and fund the booking system, in line with sector norms. That full‑time drivers may more easily absorb the cost is an incidental economic effect of working more hours, not treatment “solely because” others are part‑time.

Third, to allow claims wherever part‑time status is merely one among many reasons would collapse the distinction between direct discrimination—which the Directive covers—and indirect discrimination—which it conspicuously omits. Any generally applicable charging model would become vulnerable whenever part‑timers are differently impacted, contrary to the Directive’s intent to avoid undue burdens on employers.

Because Reeves cannot demonstrate that his part‑time status alone triggered the uniform circuit fee, his complaint falls outside Regulation 5 properly construed, and Stone Rides Inc should succeed.

Stone Rides Inc should prevail because the statutory scheme must be interpreted consistently with Directive 97/81 and its Framework Agreement, which expressly prohibits less favourable treatment “solely because” the worker is part‑time. That formulation reflects a deliberate, negotiated limit on Member States’ obligations: it targets direct, status‑based discrimination, not any business practice that may happen to impact part‑time workers more heavily.

The 2000 Regulations implement that Framework Agreement and cannot properly be read to expand materially beyond it. The phrase “on the ground that” in the Regulations must therefore be construed in harmony with “solely because” in the Directive. To detach the domestic wording from the Directive’s clear causal requirement would subvert the agreed balance between protecting part‑time workers and preserving employers’ ability to adopt neutral, commercially driven policies.

On the facts, Stone Rides applied a single, uniform “circuit fee” to all drivers, irrespective of hours worked. The undisputed principal reason for the fee was revenue generation and access to the booking system, in line with sector norms. That is a classic general business rationale, not a classification based on part‑time status. Any differential economic impact on part‑time workers arises from their lower usage, not from being labelled “part‑time” nor from any term that treats them less favourably as such.

Reeves’ case effectively invites the court to recognise an indirect‑discrimination style claim under Regulations that, as the Framework Agreement confirms, were not intended to encompass indirect discrimination. Requiring proof that part‑time status was the sole operative reason preserves that boundary and avoids converting every neutral fee or uniform condition into potential litigation whenever part‑timers are disproportionately affected.

Accordingly, as the fee was not imposed “solely because” Reeves was part‑time, his claim must fail and Stone Rides Inc should succeed.

The court’s paramount consideration is Child S’s welfare now and in the foreseeable future. On the evidence, Child S is thriving in Ms. Samuels’s care within a structured, professionally monitored placement. That offers a direct, contemporaneous window into Ms. Samuels’s actual parenting, her capacity to regulate her emotions, and any impact of her mental health or historic drug use. That real‑time evidence is inherently more probative of current and future risk than attempting to reconstruct events from years ago, when Ms. Samuels was herself a minor in a conflicted household.

A full fact‑finding into Child R’s death would be complex, heavily contested, and intrinsically uncertain: injuries “sometimes associated” with shaking or impact, no criminal conviction, and dated medical and witness evidence. Such a process risks yielding equivocal findings that are of limited additional value beyond the court’s existing knowledge that an unexplained death occurred in difficult circumstances. The court already can and will factor that historic concern into risk assessments without turning the care proceedings for Child S into an inquest on the past.

Children Act 1989 principles, reinforced by appellate authority, require that case management decisions be proportionate, avoid unnecessary delay, and focus on what is necessary to resolve the issues relevant to the subject child. Here, an extensive historical inquiry would materially prolong proceedings, divert Ms. Samuels’s emotional and practical energies away from parenting, and thereby itself risk harming Child S’s emotional security—despite no present evidence of harm.

The court has ample, reliable, and directly relevant material on Ms. Samuels’s current functioning. It should exercise its discretion to decline further fact‑finding and determine Child S’s future on the basis of present circumstances and forward‑looking assessments.

The court should decline a further fact‑finding into Child R’s death because it is not necessary or proportionate to determining Child S’s welfare under the Children Act 1989.

First, the court’s paramount consideration is Child S’s current welfare (s.1(1)). Child S is thriving in Ms. Samuels’s care within a closely monitored residential placement. Professionals already have, and can further obtain, robust evidence about Ms. Samuels’s present parenting, mental health, and risk factors through direct observation, structured assessments, and expert input. That evidence goes directly to the key statutory questions; a historical inquiry would be, at best, indirect and speculative.

Second, proportionality and the need to avoid delay (s.1(2) and Article 8 ECHR) militate strongly against a time‑consuming re‑litigation of events years in the past, when Ms. Samuels was herself a traumatized minor. The evidential picture around Child R’s death is inherently weak: no criminal conviction, injuries consistent with but not determinative of non‑accidental harm, and degraded memories. There is a real risk that a lengthy hearing would produce ambiguous findings that add little, while significantly delaying final decisions for Child S.

Third, past harm is relevant only insofar as it materially informs present risk. Here, the local authority already knows the pertinent background: an unexplained death, historical instability, drug use, and anger. Those concerns are fully reflected in current assessments and can be weighed without formal attribution of culpability, in line with authorities recognizing the court’s discretion to bypass fact‑finding where it would not materially assist risk evaluation.

Finally, the process itself poses risk: prolonged, adversarial scrutiny of Ms. Samuels’s teenage conduct is likely to destabilize her, undermining the very parenting the court is required to safeguard. A focused, contemporaneous assessment of Ms. Samuels with Child S better serves the statutory objectives and Child S’s best interests.

The court is not required to undertake every conceivable inquiry into historic events; it must undertake those that are necessary and proportionate to determining Child S’s welfare under the Children Act 1989.

Here, the decisive evidence about future risk is plainly Ms. Samuels’s *current* functioning: her day‑to‑day care of Child S, her response to stress within the residential assessment, her engagement with mental‑health treatment, and professional observations over time. Child S is thriving in her care under robust, ongoing professional scrutiny. The Local Authority already has ample material to conduct an evidence‑based risk assessment focused on the child before the court.

By contrast, reopening the unexplained death of Child R years later—when Ms. Samuels was herself a minor, in a very different environment, and where no criminal or family court findings were ever made—would almost inevitably produce equivocal conclusions. At best it could yield a “not proven either way” outcome, adding little to what is already known: that there is a historic, unquantified concern which professionals must weigh. That concern is already being taken into account in current assessments.

A complex fact‑finding hearing here would be lengthy, intrusive, and of doubtful forensic value. It would, however, have clear negative consequences: substantial delay, increased stress on a vulnerable young mother with chronic trauma, and consequent emotional impact on a very young child. That is contrary to the statutory obligation to avoid delay (s.1(2) Children Act) and to act proportionately, as reinforced by Article 8 ECHR and the case‑law warning against sprawling historical inquiries where the link to present safety is weak and speculative.

The court can safely and lawfully determine Child S’s future on the basis of present evidence. A fact‑finding into Child R’s death is not necessary, not proportionate, and not in Child S’s best interests.

The court is not required to pursue every conceivable historical enquiry; it must determine what is necessary and proportionate to safeguard the specific child before it. Here, all relevant risks to Child S can be robustly assessed by reference to Ms. Samuels’s present functioning, mental health, and observed parenting, without reopening traumatic and largely unresolvable events from years ago.

First, any fact‑finding into Child R’s death would be inherently weak and speculative. The incident occurred when Ms. Samuels was a minor, evidence has significantly deteriorated, and no criminal court was able to reach a conclusive determination. A fresh inquiry is unlikely to yield clear, reliable findings capable of materially improving risk assessment beyond what is already known: that there was an unexplained death with injuries that *might* be non‑accidental. That baseline concern is already fully factored into current assessments.

Second, Child S is presently thriving in Ms. Samuels’s care under professional scrutiny. The Local Authority has access to detailed, contemporaneous observation of her parenting, validated psychological assessments, and structured risk‑assessment tools that incorporate her history, trauma, and impulsivity. Those are the most probative indicators of future risk. Case law under the Children Act 1989 and the court’s obligation to act proportionately support focusing on current, evidence‑based risk, not on attempting to prove historic allegations that add little to what is already assumed in any event.

Third, a lengthy, adversarial fact‑finding would create delay and intense stress for Ms. Samuels, undermining her fragile mental health and directly impacting Child S’s emotional security. The welfare principle and the requirement to avoid delay (s.1(2) Children Act 1989; Art. 8 ECHR proportionality) militate against such a course where it is not strictly necessary.

Accordingly, the court should decline a fact‑finding hearing into Child R’s death and concentrate on Ms. Samuels’s current, demonstrably protective care of Child S.

The court is not required to conduct every inquiry that might conceivably shed light on risk; it must conduct those that are necessary and proportionate to determining Child S’s welfare under the Children Act 1989.

Here, all the relevant *present* risk factors can be robustly assessed without reopening the circumstances of Child R’s death years ago, when Ms. Samuels was herself a minor and living in a wholly different familial context. The Local Authority already has: (i) full medical records from Child R’s case, (ii) Ms. Samuels’s mental health history and current diagnosis, (iii) evidence of her historic and current cannabis use, and (iv) direct observation of her parenting of Child S in a residential assessment.

Those materials permit a comprehensive, evidence‑based assessment of whether Ms. Samuels now presents a likelihood of significant harm. Modern risk‑assessment tools and clinical evaluations explicitly incorporate past trauma, impulsivity and aggression; they do not depend on a criminal‑style attribution of culpability for a historic, unexplained death.

By contrast, a complex fact‑finding about Child R would be speculative, resource‑intensive and slow. Leading authorities emphasise (a) that findings about long‑past events should be undertaken only where “necessary to resolve the current proceedings”, and (b) the court’s positive obligation to avoid delay (Children Act 1989, s.1(2); s.32; and Article 8 ECHR proportionality). Here, Child S is thriving in Ms. Samuels’s care under professional oversight. Prolonged, adversarial litigation around an historic tragedy will divert Ms. Samuels from her parenting, increase stress, and thereby create the very emotional risk the system is meant to avert.

The court’s task is to decide whether Child S can safely remain with her mother now. That question can, and should, be answered by focused evaluation of current functioning and supports, not by a speculative reconstruction of events years past. Accordingly, no further fact‑finding into Child R’s death is necessary or proportionate.

The court’s paramount duty under the Children Act 1989 is to protect Child S from the risk of significant harm. That exercise must be rooted in established facts, not assumptions. Here, the prior death of Child R, with injuries of a type associated with shaking or impact trauma, is a gravely serious, unexplained event. It is not peripheral background; it goes to the heart of whether there is a real, ongoing risk to Child S in Ms. Samuels’s care.

Authorities such as Re H (Minors) (Sexual Abuse: Standard of Proof) and later appellate guidance make clear that, where very serious past harm is relied upon as the foundation for future risk, the court should, so far as possible, decide whether that harm occurred and who, if anyone, was responsible. Professionals are otherwise left to work on the basis of suspicion or “unknown causation,” which is precisely what the jurisprudence warns against when the consequence may be a child remaining in, or being returned to, a dangerous situation.

Proportionality does not mean avoiding difficult inquiries; it means matching the depth of investigation to the gravity and likelihood of the risk. A non‑accidental death of a sibling is among the highest risk indicators in child protection. In that context, a focused fact‑finding hearing is not a disproportionate use of time and resources; it is indispensable.

Nor can current observations of thriving be treated as determinative. Many children appear well until a single catastrophic episode occurs. If Ms. Samuels was not responsible for Child R’s injuries, she stands to be exonerated by a careful forensic process. If she was, Child S requires robust protective measures now. Only a fact‑finding into Child R’s death can give the court the evidential foundation necessary to discharge its protective duty to Child S.

The court’s paramount consideration under s.1 Children Act 1989 is Child S’s safety and welfare, not Ms. Samuels’s understandable wish to avoid revisiting painful history. Where there has been an earlier unexplained child death with injuries characteristic of shaking or impact trauma, the law requires a risk assessment grounded in facts, not assumptions.

Authorities such as Re H (Minors) [1996] AC 563 and Re S-B [2009] UKSC 17 make clear that:  
- past harm, especially grave harm, is often the best predictor of future risk; and  
- the court must decide, on the balance of probabilities, whether such harm was inflicted and by whom, rather than leaving matters in a cloud of suspicion.

Here, the alleged past harm is at the most serious end of the spectrum: a dead infant with suspicious injuries, in the sole care of a very young mother with contemporaneous evidence of anger, instability and drug use. If Ms. Samuels did inflict or permit non‑accidental injury, that fact is central to any realistic evaluation of risk to Child S. Conversely, if she did not, a clear exoneration would materially reduce the perceived risk and permit more confident planning for Child S’s future.

Proportionality does not justify avoiding a fact‑finding hearing. The gravity of a potential recurrent pattern of lethal harm plainly outweighs the disadvantages of forensic inquiry and the inevitable delay. Section 32 CA 1989 and the 26‑week timetable do not prevent necessary fact‑finding in complex, high‑risk cases; they require that such hearings be tightly managed, not that they be abandoned.

Without firm findings about Child R’s death, the court and professionals must either under‑protect or over‑interfere with Child S’s life on the basis of conjecture. A focused fact‑finding hearing is therefore necessary, proportionate, and mandated by the child’s paramount welfare.

The court should direct a fact‑finding hearing into Child R’s death because, on these facts, it is necessary, proportionate, and squarely required by the statutory framework.

First, under s.31 Children Act 1989 the court must determine whether Child S is “likely to suffer significant harm.” Where the alleged prior harm is the unexplained death of a sibling with injuries compatible with shaking/impact, the gravity is at the highest end of the spectrum. Consistent with authorities such as Re H and Re S‑B, the assessment of “likelihood” must be rooted in proved facts, not unresolved suspicions. Without findings on Child R’s death, any evaluation of current risk to Child S rests on speculation.

Second, professional assessments of Ms. Samuels’s present parenting cannot fill this evidential gap. Risk tools and clinical evaluations must be anchored in an accurate understanding of past harm. If Ms. Samuels did inflict or contribute to non‑accidental injuries causing a child’s death, that is a profound and enduring risk factor; if she did not, that substantially changes the risk picture. Only a transparent fact‑finding exercise can distinguish these possibilities.

Third, proportionality and welfare under Articles 6 and 8 ECHR support, rather than undermine, fact‑finding here. Delay is regrettable but cannot outweigh the need to safeguard a living child from a potential recurrence of fatal harm. A time‑limited, focused inquiry into Child R’s death is a proportionate step to avoid both unnecessary removal (if risk is overstated) and catastrophic error (if risk is understated).

Finally, Ms. Samuels’s own interests are served by clear findings: either exoneration or a defined evidential basis on which support, supervision, and realistic planning for Child S can be structured. The Local Authority’s application for a fact‑finding hearing should therefore be granted.

The court cannot safely determine Child S’s future without reliable findings about Child R’s death. Under s.31 Children Act 1989, the threshold of “significant harm” and the “likelihood” of future harm must be grounded in proved facts, not suspicion. Appellate authority (e.g. Re H, Re S-B) emphasises that when grave past harm is in issue, the court must, so far as practicable, decide what happened and who, if anyone, was responsible.

Here, a previous infant in Ms. Samuels’s sole care died with injuries “sometimes associated with shaking or impact trauma.” That is the most serious category of non‑accidental harm. The Local Authority’s current risk assessment of Child S is necessarily built on shifting sand unless the court determines whether Child R’s injuries were accidental, inflicted by Ms. Samuels, or inflicted by someone else. Each scenario generates a radically different risk profile for Child S.

Proportionality does not justify avoiding this inquiry: the greater the potential harm, the more extensive the fact‑finding the court is required to undertake. Any delay or emotional strain must be weighed against the catastrophic consequence if a repeat event occurs and the court has declined to investigate clear indicators of serious past harm. Child S’s welfare—paramount under s.1 CA 1989—demands certainty as far as achievable.

Nor can presentationally “good” current care displace the need to understand whether Ms. Samuels has, in the past, caused or failed to protect a child from fatal injury. Many abusive patterns are episodic and may not be evident in a time‑limited assessment environment, particularly where professionals’ vigilance is heightened.

A focused fact‑finding hearing into Child R’s death is therefore necessary, fair, and proportionate. Only with clear findings can the court and professionals lawfully, and safely, assess the ongoing risk to Child S.

The court should accede to the Local Authority’s application for a fact‑finding hearing into Child R’s death because, on these facts, it is necessary, proportionate and integral to a lawful risk assessment for Child S.

First, the threshold under s.31 Children Act 1989 turns on whether Child S “is likely to suffer significant harm,” a prediction which must be grounded in “findings of actual fact, not mere suspicion” (cf. Re H; Re S‑B). Here, the only known episode of potential intra‑familial harm is the unexplained, fatal, non‑accidental‑type injuries to Child R while in Ms. Samuels’s care. The gravity and unusual nature of those injuries make that incident the single most probative event for assessing future risk. To ignore or leave it in a fog of uncertainty would be to base the risk assessment on hypothesis rather than established fact.

Second, where the alleged past harm is as serious as a child’s death with injuries consistent with shaking/impact trauma, Strasbourg and domestic authorities require the court to give particularly cogent reasons for either accepting or discounting that history when determining the proportionality of any protective measures under Article 8 ECHR. That demands a transparent forensic examination, not informal impressions.

Third, proportionality does not equate to avoiding all delay. The welfare of Child S is paramount, and the potential risk—repetition of fatal injury—could not be more serious. A properly timetabled fact‑finding, focused on Child R’s death, is a necessary investigative tool to avoid both under‑ and over‑protection. Without it, professionals are left to manage Child S’s safety on the basis of untested, contested allegations, which is precisely what the case law cautions against.

Accordingly, the Local Authority’s position—that only a structured fact‑finding into Child R’s death can underpin a safe, lawful risk evaluation for Child S—should prevail.

The Secretary of State should prevail because Mr Ho has not discharged even the lower standard of proof required in protection claims, properly applying the Asylum and Immigration (Treatment of Claimants, etc.) Act 2004 and relevant country evidence.

First, credibility is fundamentally compromised. Mr Ho accepts giving different, mutually inconsistent explanations for his injuries to medical staff. That inconsistency was not the product of translation or misunderstanding but a deliberate choice, which goes directly to his reliability on the very harm he now invokes. The documentary records from River Clinic and Maple District Hospital therefore do not support his account of persecution; they merely show injuries, not their cause. There is no independent corroboration of the alleged bribe demands, no proof of payments, and no contemporaneous report to any authority or independent body.

Second, the central plank of his narrative – the supposed necessity to pay bribes to avoid military service – is undermined by his father’s recognised martyr status, which, on the objective country material, secures exemption from conscription. The existence of a clear statutory exemption, operating nationwide, renders implausible the assertion that he faced unavoidable, repeated extortion specifically on that basis. At most, his account suggests ordinary criminality or local corruption, not persecution for a Convention reason.

Third, section 8 of the 2004 Act requires his late claim to be treated as damaging to his credibility. Mr Ho spent a substantial period in the UK, including through criminal proceedings and imprisonment, yet sought asylum only when faced with deportation. His proffered explanations—confusion, fear, and ignorance of procedure—are generic and unsupported, and do not displace the statutory presumption that delay undermines his account.

Given the serious criminality justifying deportation, the absence of a coherent, well‑supported narrative of Convention persecution, and the availability of state protection in Vietnam, the Secretary of State lawfully refused his protection claim.

The Secretary of State should prevail because Mr Ho has not met even the relatively low standard of a “reasonable degree of likelihood” of future persecution.

First, his core narrative is not credible. The uncontested evidence is that, by virtue of his father’s martyr status, he had no genuine liability for military service. His protection claim is premised on being pressured to pay bribes to avoid service that, on the documentary record, he was never at risk of being compelled to perform. That goes to the heart of the claim, not a peripheral inconsistency.

Second, his explanations for the injuries recorded by River Clinic and Maple District Hospital are inherently unreliable. He accepts that he gave false accounts to medical staff. A claimant who is prepared to lie to professionals about central matters of causation cannot simply insist that the tribunal now accept a different, self‑serving version, particularly in the absence of any corroborative material linking the injuries to the alleged persecutors.

Third, there is no objective evidence of the supposed bribe demands or of any attempt to engage the authorities. The country material shows that Vietnam has a functioning legal system, formal exemption regimes linked to martyr status, and anti‑corruption mechanisms. On settled asylum jurisprudence, where there is in principle a sufficiency of state protection, a claimant must demonstrate why it is ineffective for him personally. Mr Ho has not done so, relying only on generalised assertions about “local power networks”.

Fourth, section 8 of the Asylum and Immigration (Treatment of Claimants, etc.) Act 2004 requires the late making of a claim—here only after criminal conviction and service of a deportation notice—to be treated as damaging to credibility. His extensive criminality for cannabis production, committed shortly after his unlawful disembarkation, further underscores a willingness to flout legal norms.

Cumulatively, the Secretary of State was plainly entitled to reject the claim; removal would be lawful.

Mr. Ho has not discharged even the relatively low burden of demonstrating a real risk of persecution on return to Vietnam.

First, the core of his claim is internally incoherent. He accepts that, by virtue of his father’s martyr status, he was not in fact liable for conscription. That is consistent with objective country material and undermines the very premise that officials or “local networks” could legitimately leverage compulsory military service to extort annual bribes. His explanation—that corruption operated entirely outside the legal framework yet remained focused on a non‑existent obligation—relies on speculation, not evidence.

Second, the documentary record is fatally weak. The medical notes from River Clinic and Maple District Hospital do no more than confirm injuries; they do not link those injuries to persecution for a Convention reason, nor to any actor of persecution. Mr. Ho concedes he gave false accounts to medical staff, which both severs any evidential chain and shows a willingness to misrepresent material facts when convenient. That is plainly relevant to overall credibility.

Third, Mr. Ho failed to seek protection from the authorities or make any complaint, despite relying on a narrative of repeated, organised extortion. The legal framework in Vietnam, including established grievance and anti‑corruption mechanisms, provides a sufficiency of protection in the absence of cogent evidence to the contrary. His bare assertion that all remedies were futile, without concrete attempts or corroboration, is inadequate.

Fourth, his protection claim was lodged only once deportation action commenced. Under the Asylum and Immigration (Treatment of Claimants, etc.) Act 2004, that delay must be treated as damaging to credibility unless satisfactorily explained. His generalized references to “confusion” and fear are insufficient to overcome the statutory presumption, especially given his prior criminal conduct and established familiarity with official processes.

Taken cumulatively, the inconsistencies, lack of corroboration, and late claim mean Mr. Ho has not shown a real risk of persecution or serious harm. The Secretary of State’s decision was lawful and should be upheld.

The Secretary of State should prevail because Mr. Ho has not discharged even the relatively low burden of showing a “real risk” of persecution on return.

First, the core of his claim – that he was subjected to extortion and violence linked to military service – is directly undermined by objective material. Unchallenged official documentation confirms that his father’s martyr status exempted him from conscription. That is inconsistent with the alleged continuing leverage over him via military obligations. Where a claimant’s narrative conflicts with cogent documentary evidence, the Tribunal is entitled to find his account not credible.

Second, Mr. Ho’s conduct and evidence fall squarely within the credibility concerns identified in the Asylum and Immigration (Treatment of Claimants, etc.) Act 2004. He raised protection issues only after being notified of deportation, despite having been in the UK for a substantial period and having legal representation in serious criminal proceedings. Section 8 requires that such delay be treated as damaging to credibility. His inconsistent explanations for his injuries to medical staff, and the absence of any evidence of bribe payments or attempts to seek protection from higher-level or central authorities, further undermine his assertions.

Third, the background evidence regarding Vietnam records a functioning legal framework, military exemption regime and anti‑corruption mechanisms. The test is not whether corruption exists in parts of Vietnam, but whether the state is “unable or unwilling” to provide protection. Mr. Ho has provided no reliable evidence that he ever attempted to invoke these remedies or that they would be futile in his particular case.

Finally, his serious criminality in the UK is a relevant public‑interest factor. In the absence of a substantiated risk of Convention harm, the Secretary of State’s decision to refuse protection and proceed with deportation is lawful, rational and should be upheld.

The appeal should be dismissed because Mr Ho has not discharged even the relatively low burden of showing a real risk of persecution on return.

First, his core narrative is intrinsically implausible when set against objective evidence. The undisputed martyr status of his father, and the consequent exemption from conscription under Vietnamese law, fatally undermines his account that he was under compulsion to pay annual bribes to avoid military service. Faced with this, Mr Ho offers only speculation about local corruption, unsupported by any concrete examples, documents, or complaints.

Second, his credibility is seriously damaged by multiple, material inconsistencies. He accepts giving different explanations for his injuries to River Clinic and Maple District Hospital, allegedly out of fear, yet provides no corroboration that such fear existed or that the supposed persecutors had any reach into those facilities. The medical notes, on his own case, are therefore inconsistent with his protection narrative, and the Tribunal is entitled to treat them as neutral or adverse, not supportive.

Third, under the Asylum and Immigration (Treatment of Claimants, etc.) Act 2004, his very late claim—advanced only after he was served with notice of intention to deport following a serious drugs offence—is a significant adverse credibility factor. He offers vague references to confusion and fear, but he was plainly capable of engaging with UK authorities in the criminal process and of obtaining legal advice; there is no satisfactory reason why a person genuinely in fear would wait until removal became imminent.

Fourth, Mr Ho has never sought protection from the Vietnamese authorities or higher-level bodies, despite the existence of legal and administrative remedies and anti‑corruption mechanisms. Country information does not show a systemic inability or unwillingness to protect someone in his position.

Cumulatively, the inconsistencies, absence of corroboration, and late claim mean the lower standard of proof is not met. The Secretary of State’s decision should be upheld.

Mr. Ho’s claim must be assessed under the lower “real risk/reasonable degree of likelihood” standard, not the criminal standard, and on the evidence as a whole. On that basis, he meets the test.

First, his core account has remained consistent: because of issues linked to military service exemption and his father’s martyr status, powerful local actors repeatedly targeted him for bribes and assaulted him. The Secretary of State does not dispute the existence of a conscription system, martyr exemptions, or corruption in Vietnam; the dispute is whether these matters affected this particular man. That is precisely where the corroboration matters.

The medical records from River Clinic and Maple District Hospital are independent, contemporaneous documentation of injuries consistent with his account of repeated assaults. His explanation for giving benign causes to hospital staff is inherently plausible in a context where assailants are linked to local power networks and retaliation is feared. Country material on Vietnam supports the proposition that local corruption can in practice nullify formal protections and deter complaints, rendering state protection ineffective in particular regions.

The absence of formal complaints or receipts for bribes is not surprising in such a setting and cannot reasonably be treated as fatal where there is some corroboration and credible explanation for gaps. Nor does the late timing of the asylum claim, while relevant under the 2004 Act, automatically destroy credibility; delay must be weighed against his fear for family, confusion about legal options, and his precarious status after criminal proceedings.

Crucially, the Secretary of State has not displaced the core question: is there a real risk that, on return, the same actors—operating with impunity—could resume extortion and violence? On the cumulative evidence, and in light of acknowledged difficulties in accessing effective protection in corrupt localities, that threshold is plainly met. Mr. Ho is entitled to protection.

Mr. Ho’s claim meets the applicable “real risk” / “reasonable degree of likelihood” standard and should be allowed.

First, credibility must be assessed holistically, not mechanistically against an idealised evidential record. Mr. Ho offers a coherent core narrative: local actors exploited ambiguity around conscription, leveraging his father’s martyr status as a pretext for regular extortion, and repeatedly assaulted him when he resisted. That account is directly supported by two independent medical records from River Clinic and Maple District Hospital in Ho Chi Minh City, each contemporaneous with injuries that are entirely consistent with his claimed beatings. His explanation for giving false causes to medical staff – fear of reprisals from attackers linked to local power networks – is both plausible and consistent with country evidence on corruption and the risks of complaining about powerful actors.

Second, the Secretary of State’s reliance on the formal legal framework in Vietnam is misplaced. The question is not whether remedies exist in law, but whether they are practically effective for this claimant. Credible background evidence of systemic corruption and local impunity in parts of Vietnam shows that persons in conflict with such networks cannot reasonably be expected to seek protection, still less obtain it. A theoretical right to complain does not defeat a protection claim where doing so would be futile or dangerous.

Third, delay and limited documentation do not, under the 2004 Act, automatically destroy credibility. They are factors, but must be weighed against Mr. Ho’s unchallenged vulnerability as a foreign seafarer turned irregular migrant, his lack of legal knowledge, his expressed fear of endangering family in Vietnam, and the corroborative medical evidence. Many recognised refugees only claim once removal becomes imminent; that timing is common, not inherently suspect.

Taken cumulatively, Mr. Ho’s evidence easily crosses the low threshold: there is a real risk of renewed extortion and serious harm by non‑state actors against whom the Vietnamese state cannot or will not provide effective protection. His appeal should be allowed.

Mr. Ho satisfies the protection standard when the evidence is assessed cumulatively and in accordance with the correct, low standard of proof: a “reasonable degree of likelihood” of persecution on return.

His explanations—fear for his family, confusion about legal processes, and precarious immigration status after criminal conviction—are entirely consistent with the behaviour of many genuine refugees. The delay cannot outweigh the medical evidence, his detailed narrative, and the acknowledged reality of corruption in parts of Vietnam.

Mr. Ho’s claim must be assessed under the correct, *low* standard of proof: whether there is a “reasonable degree of likelihood” of persecution or serious harm on return, not whether his account is proved on a balance of probabilities or beyond reasonable doubt. On that standard, his evidence, taken cumulatively, is sufficient.

First, his core narrative is consistent and plausibly anchored in country conditions. Credible reporting recognises entrenched corruption, local patronage networks, and abuses around conscription exemptions in Vietnam. The Secretary of State relies on the *existence* of legal frameworks and anti‑corruption measures, but asylum law recognises that what matters is *effective protection in practice*. His explanation for giving false causes to hospital staff – fear of retribution by the very actors who control his environment – is both rational and squarely in line with recognised behaviour of victims of organised abuse. Apparent discrepancies in accounts of causation therefore do not defeat his claim; they are part of the evidential picture that the lower standard of proof is designed to accommodate.

Third, the late timing of his asylum claim is, under the 2004 Act, a factor in credibility but not determinative. He provided plausible reasons: confusion about procedure, fear for his family, and distrust of authorities due to his prior experiences. The weight of authority cautions against allowing delay alone to negate an otherwise credible risk.

Finally, his criminal conviction cannot justify refoulement where there remains a real risk of serious harm. On the totality of the evidence, Mr. Ho has shown such a risk and should be granted protection.

The Tribunal must apply the “real risk” / “reasonable degree of likelihood” standard, not balance‑of‑probabilities. On that standard, Mr. Ho’s evidence, viewed cumulatively and in context, is sufficient.

First, the medical records from River Clinic and Maple District Hospital are independent, contemporaneous documents from different institutions in Vietnam. They objectively confirm that he sustained significant injuries in-country, consistent with his account of repeated assaults. Minor discrepancies in how he explained those injuries to hospital staff are entirely explicable: he reasonably feared that disclosing politically‑sensitive extortion linked to military exemptions could expose him and his family to further retaliation in a system where corrupt local actors can exercise de facto power.

Second, the Secretary of State’s reliance on the formal legal framework in Vietnam is misplaced. The issue is not whether remedies exist on paper but whether they are practically accessible to Mr. Ho, given the very influence networks and corruption he describes. It is well recognised in protection jurisprudence that where the persecutors are connected to or shielded by local officials, recourse to the state can be futile or dangerous; the absence of complaints or “official” protection‑seeking is therefore not determinative.

Third, the Asylum and Immigration (Treatment of Claimants, etc.) Act 2004 requires late claims to be considered as a factor in credibility, not an automatic bar. Mr. Ho’s explanation—limited English, lack of legal understanding, focus on criminal proceedings, and fear of blowback on relatives in Vietnam—is plausible and consistent with the psychological reality of traumatised migrants. His subsequent account has been detailed and internally coherent.

Finally, his father’s martyr status is a double‑edged factor: while it should in theory exempt him from service, it also enhances the plausibility of informal demands for “payments” to secure or confirm that exemption in a corrupt local environment.

On the lower standard of proof, these elements establish a real risk of future harm. Protection should be granted.

Jade Energy Ventures’ disposal of Iris House is a classic transaction at an undervalue within section 423.

First, Jade was the registered legal owner. Unless and until an effective trust divested that beneficial interest, Iris House formed part of the asset pool available to creditors. Section 53(1)(b) LPA 1925 requires that any declaration of trust of land be “manifested and proved” in writing signed by the person able to declare it – here, Jade as landowner. Authorities construing both section 53(1)(b) and its predecessors stress strict formal compliance to prevent exactly what Jade attempts: deploying vague, ex post “beneficial ownership” claims to defeat creditors.

Jade cannot rely on informal foreign-law arrangements or oral understandings. Any such arrangement, insofar as it concerns English land, must satisfy English formality rules. Nor can it cure the defect by pointing to later mortgage documents: these are, at most, references to an asserted pre-existing trust, not a clear declaration by Jade that it holds Iris House on trust for Emerald. They do not identify trust terms or unequivocally divest Jade of its beneficial interest. Critically, Steel Horizon is entitled to insist on compliance with section 53(1)(b)’s evidential safeguards; “imperfect” or incomplete documentation is precisely what the statute is designed to neutralise.

Further, the identity and capacity of the signatory matters. A company acts through properly authorised organs. If the alleged declarations were signed in the context of mortgage transactions, not as trust declarations by Jade qua trustee, they cannot retroactively re‑characterise Jade’s beneficial ownership. To relax this requirement invites fraud on creditors.

Finally, the timing is damning: transfer followed immediately upon Steel Horizon’s enforcement efforts. Absent a valid prior trust, the transfer stripped Jade of a valuable asset for no consideration, plainly with a purpose to put Iris House beyond creditors’ reach. Section 423 is engaged; the transaction should be set aside in Steel Horizon’s favour.

Iris House was an asset standing in Jade Energy’s name and available to meet its creditors unless Jade proves a prior, validly constituted trust in favor of Emerald. It has not done so.

Section 53(1)(b) LPA 1925 is not a casual evidential rule; it is a formal requirement designed to prevent precisely the kind of ex post facto, document‑based reconstruction now advanced. A declaration of trust “respecting any land” is unenforceable unless “manifested and proved by some writing signed by some person who is able to declare such trust.” That must be the legal owner (here, Jade), not merely anyone who can sign some document mentioning a supposed beneficial owner.

The mortgage‑related documents do not amount to a compliant declaration of trust. They are transactional securities, not instruments by which Jade, as trustee, clearly declares that it holds Iris House for Emerald. At best, they are ambiguous references to Emerald’s economic involvement. Section 53(1)(b) requires clear manifestation that Jade is divesting its beneficial interest; it is not satisfied by incidental or inferential language in finance documents whose purpose is entirely different.

Jade’s reliance on an earlier “arrangement under foreign law” is likewise defective: no cogent evidence shows a trust of English land that meets English formalities. A purported oral or incomplete trust can neither diminish the beneficial estate nor defeat section 423 creditors’ remedies.

Accordingly, Iris House was Jade’s asset when Steel Horizon’s claim arose. The subsequent transfer to Emerald for no, or grossly inadequate, consideration shortly after Steel Horizon obtained permission to enforce the award is paradigmatic of a transaction at an undervalue under section 423, carried out with the purpose of putting assets beyond creditors’ reach. The court should so hold and grant Steel Horizon relief restoring Iris House (or its value) to Jade’s estate.

Jade Energy Ventures’ disposition of Iris House is plainly a transaction at an undervalue within section 423.

First, Jade bears the burden of displacing the obvious position: Iris House stood on its balance sheet as a free asset until it was transferred away, for no consideration, shortly after Steel Horizon obtained permission to enforce a substantial award. That is the paradigm mischief at which section 423 is aimed.

To avoid this, Jade must show that it never beneficially owned Iris House—that it was already held on trust for Emerald Pension Fund. That contention fails on formal and evidential grounds.

Section 53(1)(b) LPA 1925 requires that a declaration of trust of land “be manifested and proved by some writing signed by some person who is able to declare such trust.” The statute is protective: it prevents exactly the kind of retrospective, undocumented “trust” now asserted against creditors. Authorities under section 53(1)(b) and its predecessors emphasise strict compliance. Oral understandings, informal arrangements under foreign law, or incomplete paperwork cannot divest the legal owner’s beneficial interest in English land as against third parties.

The two mortgage-related documents do not amount to a compliant declaration: they are not framed as trust instruments, do not clearly identify the terms or subject matter of any trust, and were signed in the context of financing, not as manifestations of a pre‑existing equitable ownership. Critically, there is no clear signature by Jade in its capacity as settlor declaring that it henceforth holds Iris House for Emerald Pension Fund. To treat routine corporate signatures on security documents as satisfying section 53(1)(b) would gut the statute of its function.

Accordingly, Jade remained beneficially entitled to Iris House until it gifted the property away. That disposal depleted Jade’s estate and was timed and structured to defeat Steel Horizon’s enforcement. Section 423 is therefore engaged and the transaction must be unwound.

Jade Energy Ventures’ transfer of Iris House is a transaction at an undervalue within section 423.

First, Jade Energy Ventures was the registered legal owner. Absent a valid, enforceable trust in favor of Emerald Pension Fund, Iris House formed part of Jade Energy Ventures’ asset base available to creditors, including Steel Horizon. Section 53(1)(b) LPA 1925 is not a mere evidential nicety; it is a mandatory formality for the enforceability of any declaration of trust of land. The statute expressly requires a declaration “manifested and proved by some writing signed by some person who is able to declare such trust.” That must be the disponor itself (here, Jade Energy Ventures acting as beneficial owner), not simply anyone who happens to sign a document referring to a supposed beneficial interest.

The mortgage documents relied on by Jade Energy Ventures are, at best, secondary transactional paperwork; they are not a contemporaneous, clear declaration by Jade Energy Ventures that it holds Iris House on trust. Treating any reference in such documents, signed in some corporate capacity, as satisfying section 53(1)(b) would hollow out the statutory protection and re‑open the very risk of “hidden” trusts the provision was designed to prevent—particularly prejudicing creditors who rely on the register and on strict formalities.

Further, any alleged oral or informally arranged “foreign law” trust cannot diminish Jade Energy Ventures’ beneficial interest in English land without compliance with English formalities. Until a compliant, signed declaration exists, Jade Energy Ventures remains full beneficial owner.

Jade Energy Ventures’ disposal of Iris House is a textbook “transaction at an undervalue” within section 423.

They say nothing clear about a pre‑existing trust obligation, and are at best ambiguous. Ambiguity is precisely what section 53(1)(b) is designed to prevent.

Second, the statute requires a signature by “some person who is able to declare such trust,” i.e. the landowner itself, in that capacity. Jade has not shown that the signatories were acting as Jade’s mind and will in declaring a trust of Iris House, rather than as mere functionaries executing finance documents. Treating any corporate signature on collateral documents as sufficient would hollow out section 53(1)(b) and invite the very hidden arrangements the statute was enacted to preclude—especially to the detriment of creditors such as Steel Horizon.

Third, absent a properly evidenced trust, Jade held full beneficial ownership of Iris House when the arbitral award became enforceable. The subsequent transfer to Emerald Pension Fund, for no commercial consideration and timed after enforcement permission, plainly depleted Jade’s asset pool with a purpose to prejudice creditors. That is exactly the mischief section 423 seeks to remedy.

Section 423 IA 1986 is engaged only if Jade disposed of “its” asset at an undervalue with the proscribed purpose. That premise fails: Iris House was never beneficially Jade’s to deploy against creditors.

First, on the facts, Iris House was at all times held for Emerald Pension Fund under an earlier foreign-law arrangement. If beneficial title was already vested in Emerald under that arrangement, Jade’s later transfer merely perfected Emerald’s existing rights and did not diminish Jade’s estate available to Steel Horizon.

Second, even if English law formalities apply, section 53(1)(b) is evidential, not constitutive. A trust can be declared orally or informally; the statute only requires that it “be manifested and proved” in signed writing. The two mortgage-related documents do precisely that. They are contemporaneous, written acknowledgments—filed in a public registry—expressly treating Emerald as the beneficial owner. There is no policy reason to disregard such clear, signed admissions by Jade.

Third, as a company, Jade “signs” only through its authorized officers and agents. Long-established corporate law accepts that documents signed by those acting within their authority bind the company and satisfy statutory “signed by” requirements. To insist on some additional, personal signature by an abstract “landowner” would be both artificial and unworkable, and would introduce precisely the uncertainty section 53 aims to avoid.

Because Iris House was already impressed with a binding trust in Emerald’s favour, Jade had no free beneficial interest to give away at an undervalue. The section 423 claim therefore fails at the threshold: there was no relevant depletion of Jade’s assets and no transaction capable of being set aside.

Jade Energy Ventures should prevail because Iris House was never beneficially available to Steel Horizon or other creditors: it was held on trust for Emerald Pension Fund well before the complained‑of transfer, and that trust satisfies section 53(1)(b) LPA 1925.

First, section 53(1)(b) is directed to evidencing, not constituting, express trusts of land. Once a trust is validly declared (e.g. by board resolution, contractual obligation or equivalent foreign‑law arrangement), it is not rendered void simply because the written record is imperfect; later signed writings can “prove” the existing trust. The two mortgage‑related documents, signed by Jade’s authorized representatives and filed in the ordinary course of dealings with third‑party lenders, are written acknowledgments that Emerald was the beneficial owner. They are precisely the type of reliable documentary evidence the statute demands to prevent fabricated trusts.

Second, for a corporate landowner, “signed by the person able to declare the trust” necessarily includes signatures by those acting as the company’s organs or duly authorized agents. The law does not insist on some metaphysical signature by the abstract corporate entity; it looks to who has authority to bind it. Here, the representatives who signed the mortgage documents indisputably had power to encumber the property; that same authority is more than sufficient to acknowledge and confirm an existing trust.

Third, if Iris House was already held on trust, Jade never owned more than the bare legal title. A transfer of that title to the true beneficiary is not a “transaction at an undervalue” under section 423 IA 1986; it is the performance of a pre‑existing obligation that leaves Jade’s net estate unchanged. Section 423 cannot be used to enlarge a debtor’s estate beyond its genuine beneficial interests.

Accordingly, Steel Horizon fails to show any depletion of Jade’s assets, and the section 423 claim must be dismissed.

Jade Energy Ventures should prevail because, on proper analysis, Iris House was never part of its free assets: it was held on trust for Emerald Pension Fund long before any section 423 issue could arise.

First, section 53(1)(b) LPA 1925 is an evidential formality, not a requirement that the trust itself be *constituted* only by a contemporaneous signed document. Second, those documents do not create an ex post facto trust to defeat creditors; they confirm the previously existing beneficial ownership of Emerald Pension Fund. Section 53(1)(b) is satisfied if there is a sufficient written acknowledgment of the trust; it does not demand that all terms or the inception date be set out, only that the existence and subject matter of the trust be evidenced in writing. That is exactly what the mortgage documents do.

Third, section 423 IA 1986 requires a “transaction” by which the debtor’s estate is diminished. If, at all material times, Jade Energy Ventures held only bare legal title and no beneficial interest, there was no asset to put beyond Steel Horizon’s reach and no “undervalue”: the later transfer of Iris House simply perfected Emerald Pension Fund’s pre-existing equitable entitlement.

Accordingly, Iris House never formed part of Jade Energy Ventures’ realizable estate, and section 423 is not engaged. The claim should therefore be dismissed.

Jade Energy Ventures should prevail because Iris House was never part of the company’s beneficial estate available to Steel Horizon or other creditors.

First, section 53(1)(b) LPA 1925 is an evidential, not constitutive, requirement. A trust of land may be declared orally or arise under foreign-law arrangements, and remains valid in equity; section 53(1)(b) merely bars its *enforcement* absent sufficient written evidence “signed by some person who is able to declare such trust or by his will.” That language expressly contemplates signature “by some person,” not necessarily the beneficial owner personally: for a corporation, signature by duly authorized representatives is the orthodox and necessary mode of acting. The mortgage documents, executed by Jade’s authorized officers and filed publicly, are clear, unequivocal written acknowledgments that Emerald Pension Fund is the beneficial owner. They satisfy the statutory function of preventing fraud by fixing the beneficial ownership on the very documents Jade’s own officers signed and relied on.

Second, the consistent narrative—that Iris House belonged beneficially to the pension fund under the initial foreign-law arrangement, and at the latest under a trust that Jade expressly confirmed—means no “transaction at an undervalue” occurred. If Jade held no beneficial interest (or only bare legal title) at the relevant time, the subsequent transfer did nothing more than perfect an existing equitable entitlement. Completing an existing trust obligation is not an impoverishing disposition; it restores property to its true beneficial owner.

Third, Steel Horizon’s interpretation would permit creditors to defeat genuine, pre-existing trust arrangements of which there is clear written evidence, solely by insisting on hyper-technical formalism incompatible with corporate practice and the text of section 53(1)(b). That outcome would subvert, not advance, the statute’s anti-fraud purpose.

Jade Energy Ventures should succeed because Iris House was never part of its freely available asset pool: it was held beneficially for Emerald Pension Fund, and the statutory formalities have been met in substance and in law.

First, section 53(1)(b) LPA 1925 is concerned with evidencing a trust, not with constituting one exclusively by written instrument. An express trust of land may be declared orally; the statute operates to bar its *enforcement* absent written evidence signed by the person able to declare the trust.
