ShelterCo should prevail because the Building Safety Act 2022 (“BSA”) does not clearly, expressly, or necessarily operate to extinguish vested contractual and statutory rights to recover pre‑commencement costs via service charges.

First, the leases and the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 confer an established right to recover “necessary repair and remediation” and compliance costs, subject to reasonableness. Those rights crystallised as soon as ShelterCo incurred the expenditure and/or became contractually liable for it. Under orthodox principles of statutory interpretation, Parliament is presumed not to interfere retroactively with accrued rights or vested interests absent clear words or necessary implication (see, by analogy, Tunnicliffe). No such explicit transitional provision in the BSA nullifies recovery of already‑incurred costs.

Second, Schedule 8 BSA is drafted in the present and future tense, regulating what is chargeable “under a lease” going forward. Where Parliament sought to address “historical” liabilities, it did so expressly and in defined circumstances (e.g., qualifying leases, caps, landlord‑contribution conditions). That calibrated scheme is inconsistent with a sweeping, implied extinguishment of all pre‑commencement remediation and associated professional costs otherwise recoverable on orthodox service‑charge principles.

Third, interpreting the BSA to bar recovery of pre‑commencement costs would produce an arbitrary and disproportionate deprivation of ShelterCo’s property and contractual rights, contrary to established common‑law presumptions and A1P1 ECHR compatibility. Parliament intended to rebalance risk, not to expropriate legitimate, already‑incurred expenditures without clear words or compensation.

Finally, the remedial and legal‑costs elements are integral to making the building safe and to activating the very protections on which leaseholders now rely. To deny recovery would undermine the coherent operation of the BSA regime itself.

Accordingly, ShelterCo remains entitled to recover the pre‑commencement fire‑safety and remedial costs, including associated legal expenses, through the service charge machinery in the existing leases.

ShelterCo’s claim fails because the Building Safety Act 2022 (“BSA”) was expressly designed to break from the pre‑existing service‑charge model and to stop leaseholders at high‑rise blocks such as Lowbridge Towers bearing historic fire‑safety costs.

First, the text. Schedule 8 BSA imposes substantive limits on “relevant measures” and “remediation costs” being passed to qualifying leaseholders, and it does so by reference to *when the costs are demanded*, not when the landlord chose to incur them. The operative prohibition is forward‑looking: from commencement, demands for specified categories of cladding and fire‑safety remediation, and associated professional and legal costs, are irrecoverable via service charge. That ShelterCo incurred some items earlier is irrelevant; Parliament regulated the *charging relationship*, not the timing of the contractor’s invoice.

Secondly, statutory purpose. The BSA responds precisely to the problem ShelterCo presents: landlords relying on boiler‑plate Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 service‑charge clauses to offload life‑critical safety failures onto long‑leaseholders with no meaningful bargaining power. Hansard and government policy material emphasise a “reset” of historic risk allocation, with costs redirected to developers, landlords and public funds. Reading schedule 8 so as to preserve landlords’ ability to recover pre‑commencement historic defect costs would hollow out that reform and perpetuate the mischief.

Thirdly, the presumption against retroactivity does not assist ShelterCo. There is no attempt to undo past legal effects or reopen final accounts. The BSA simply changes, prospectively, what landlords may recover going forward, in a heavily regulated field of public safety and housing. Courts have repeatedly held (including in rent and consumer‑protection contexts) that Parliament may modify the future consequences of existing contracts where social policy demands it.

Finally, proportionality favours the Occupants. ShelterCo retains its freehold, long‑term income, and alternative recovery routes; the Occupants’ homes and solvency are at stake. Properly interpreted, schedule 8 bars ShelterCo’s claimed service‑charge recovery, and the Occupants must succeed.

Occupants should prevail because the Building Safety Act 2022 (“BSA”) is expressly designed to re‑allocate historic building‑safety risk, and its text, structure and purpose require that ShelterCo’s service‑charge recovery is now curtailed, even for many pre‑commencement costs.

First, Schedule 8 BSA is framed in mandatory, lease‑overriding terms: qualifying leaseholders “are not liable” via service charges for specified “relevant measures”, including cladding remediation and associated professional/legal costs arising from building‑safety defects. Parliament deliberately created statutory caps, exclusions and no‑recovery rules that bite “notwithstanding any term of a lease”, thereby cutting across pre‑existing contractual and Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 rights. That is classic supervening regulation of ongoing contractual relationships, not impermissible retroactivity.

Second, the statutory focus is on the nature and purpose of the expenditure, not on when each invoice was raised. The mischief was historic fire‑safety defects and their remediation burdens, already crystallised across England by 2022. Limiting the BSA to only post‑commencement costs would leave the very “historic” liabilities untouched and defeat Parliament’s central objective: to protect leaseholders in high‑risk buildings over 11m/18m from precisely these legacy safety bills.

Third, the absence of transitional language favouring landlords is neutral at best. Where Parliament has used strong, rights‑cutting language in a public‑safety context, courts routinely give it effective operation, even where it incidentally depresses the value of vested contractual rights. Authorities on public‑protection statutes confirm that they may lawfully and proportionately reshape existing bargains where justified by safety and fairness concerns. The BSA, a response to the post‑Grenfell crisis, plainly meets that standard.

Finally, any residual ambiguity must, under familiar interpretive principles, be resolved in favour of the protective purpose and against imposing heavy, technical safety costs on residential occupiers. The Court should therefore hold that ShelterCo cannot recover the disputed remediation and associated legal expenses through service charges.

The Occupants should prevail because the Building Safety Act 2022 (“BSA”) was deliberately crafted to prevent exactly this outcome: the passing of historic fire-safety failure costs to residential leaseholders via service charges, whether incurred before or after commencement.

Schedule 8 BSA imposes substantive limits on “relevant measures” and “relevant defects” in “relevant buildings” over 11m; Lowbridge Towers plainly qualifies. Those provisions are framed not as merely prospective accounting rules but as an ongoing prohibition on demanding service charges for certain categories of fire‑safety remediation and associated professional/legal costs. The trigger is the nature of the defect and the type of cost, not the precise date when the landlord first paid the invoice.

Parliament knew that most unsafe cladding and fire‑stopping problems were historic. Yet it chose sweeping language that bars recovery of remediation and connected professional costs from leaseholders, subject only to carefully crafted exceptions and caps. To read the Act as leaving all pre‑commencement expenditure outside its scope would gut its remedial purpose and frustrate the central policy of re-allocating historic burdens to developers, freeholders and the state.

There is no impermissible “retrospectivity” here. The BSA does not undo past payments; it regulates future service‑charge liability and collection. Courts have long accepted that consumer‑protection and public‑safety statutes may interfere with the exercise of pre‑existing contractual rights where Parliament clearly intends to rebalance risks (as reflected in the BSA’s Explanatory Notes, debates and the structure of schedule 8).

Nor can ShelterCo rely on silence about transitional arrangements. Where the statutory text and purpose are protective, ambiguities must be resolved in favour of the protected class. The leases and the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 are necessarily read subject to this later, more specific regime. Accordingly, ShelterCo is barred from recovering the contested remediation and associated legal costs through service charges.

ShelterCo’s claim fails because the Building Safety Act 2022 (BSA) was expressly designed to reallocate the financial burden of building safety defects away from leaseholders, including in respect of “historical” defects and associated professional and legal costs.

Schedule 8 BSA, read purposively, prohibits recovery via service charge of “relevant measures” taken in connection with fire‑safety defects in higher‑risk buildings such as Lowbridge Towers (>18m). The Schedule is not confined to post‑commencement expenditure; it focuses on the *nature* and *purpose* of the costs (remediation or related professional services) and the status of the payer (qualifying leaseholders), not the date of the outlay. Parliament could not achieve its stated goal of protecting leaseholders from historic building safety costs if landlords were free to crystallise and pass on pre‑commencement liabilities simply because work or instructions began earlier.

Any ambiguity must be resolved in light of the Act’s remedial purpose and legislative history, which emphasise shielding residential leaseholders and placing costs on developers, freeholders and the wider industry. Statutes addressing public safety and distributive fairness routinely and legitimately alter existing contractual allocations of risk. The general presumption against retrospectivity yields where Parliament clearly intends to correct a systemic injustice and does so through targeted, prospective control over *enforcement* (here, barring or limiting future service‑charge recovery), rather than undoing past transactions.

ShelterCo retains its proprietary interest and may seek alternative routes of recovery (e.g. against those responsible for defects), so there is no disproportionate deprivation of property. What is restricted is only the ability to fund historic fire‑safety failures through residential service charges.

Accordingly, the court should hold that the BSA 2022 and Schedule 8 bar ShelterCo from recovering the disputed remediation and associated legal/professional costs from the Occupants.

The Occupants should prevail because the Building Safety Act 2022 (“BSA”) was specifically designed to re‑allocate historic fire‑safety burdens away from leaseholders, and its text and structure necessarily cut across ShelterCo’s pre‑existing service‑charge rights, including for pre‑commencement expenditure.

First, Schedule 8 BSA imposes substantive limits on what “relevant measure” costs are recoverable by way of service charge in “relevant buildings” over 11 meters/5 storeys; Lowbridge Towers clearly qualifies. Those limits are framed in present‑tense terms—“no service charge is payable” in respect of certain remediation and professional costs—without any carve‑out for past spending or for demands based on earlier contractual rights. Parliament could easily have preserved historical recovery; instead it used sweeping prohibitory language.

Secondly, the legislative materials around the BSA make clear that its purpose is to prevent leaseholders from being the “first port of call” for historical safety defects, shifting liability to developers, landlords and the wider industry. Under orthodox principles of purposive construction and Pepper v Hart, that clear remedial intention justifies interpreting Schedule 8 as applying to all qualifying costs, whenever incurred, provided they are sought to be recovered after commencement.

Thirdly, there is nothing impermissibly “retrospective” about regulating future recoverability of past costs. The BSA does not unwind vested titles or invalidate completed transactions; it simply limits *future* service‑charge liabilities—an area always subject to statutory control (Landlord and Tenant Act 1985, Housing Act 1985, etc.). Courts have consistently upheld such social‑protection measures, especially where public safety and distributive fairness are in issue.

Finally, any ambiguity must be resolved in favour of the protected class. The BSA is explicit protective legislation; leaseholders are its intended beneficiaries. On that basis, the court should hold that ShelterCo cannot recover the contested remediation and associated legal/professional costs through service charges, irrespective of when those costs were incurred.

Section 28 of the Supreme Court of Judicature (Ireland) Act 1877 expressly contemplates the absolute assignment of “any debt or other legal chose in action,” which includes a cause of action in contract or tort. The claim against Hayworth Automation is a classic chose in action: it is quantified, arises from alleged breach of an exclusive distribution arrangement, and has always been treated by the parties as a transferable litigation asset worth approximately €11 million.

The statutory requirements are formal, not purposive: there must be an absolute assignment in writing, with notice to the debtor. Those elements are met. Once assigned, the cause of action becomes Mr. Cameron’s property; he sues in his own name, not as Arnext’s representative. The rules on corporate representation are therefore simply inapplicable.

Public‑policy objections based on maintenance and champerty also fail. This is not “trafficking in litigation” by a stranger; it is the assignment of a company asset to a principal shareholder and former director who was already economically exposed to the outcome. The transaction aligns the proprietary and litigation interests rather than splintering them. Modern authorities recognise that litigation claims are routinely and legitimately assigned—by liquidators, in factoring, and in other debt‑related contexts—provided that the assignee acquires a genuine proprietary interest and controls the litigation for that interest. That is precisely the position here.

Nor is there any coherent company‑law objection. The company, facing inability to fund the claim, chose the only realistic route to realise value: transferring the asset to someone willing to bear the risk and cost. Directors’ fiduciary duties are satisfied if the transaction is honestly believed to be in the company’s best interests; enabling pursuit of an €11 million claim, at no litigation cost to the company, readily meets that test.

To invalidate such an assignment would be to weaponise procedural rules against access to justice, particularly for under‑resourced companies, in direct tension with the policy of section 28.

Section 28 of the Supreme Court of Judicature (Ireland) Act 1877 expressly permits the absolute assignment of “any debt or other legal chose in action” when (i) it is in writing under the hand of the assignor, and (ii) express notice is given to the debtor. Those formal requirements are satisfied here: Arnext Controls and Engineering Limited executed written instruments assigning its cause of action, and Hayworth Automation was formally notified. Once those conditions are met, the statute does not condition validity on the assignor’s motives or on the assignee’s status.

A cause of action in contract/tort is a chose in action and a recognised item of property. Company law treats such claims as part of the company’s assets capable of sale or assignment, including to insiders, subject to fiduciary standards. Here, the assignment was not a device to strip value from Arnext but the only realistic mechanism to preserve and prosecute a potentially valuable corporate asset. Cameron, as principal shareholder, is economically aligned with the company; any recovery benefits him and, indirectly, the company and its creditors. That is the opposite of the speculative “trafficking in litigation” at which maintenance and champerty are aimed.

The champerty authorities are directed at strangers investing in litigation for profit, not at a director/shareholder assuming a company’s own claim where the company is impecunious. Public policy favours enabling meritorious claims to be heard, not extinguishing them because the corporate claimant cannot afford lawyers. To recharacterise this assignment as merely an evasion of representation rules ignores that, once assigned, the chose in action is Cameron’s personal property, and he sues in his own right.

Refusing effect to such an assignment would unduly penalise small companies and their principals, denying them effective access to the courts and depriving them of a lawful statutory mechanism expressly designed to allow assignment of claims.

Section 28 of the Supreme Court of Judicature (Ireland) Act 1877 permits the absolute assignment of “any debt or other legal chose in action” once (i) the assignment is in writing, (ii) notice is given to the debtor/defendant, and (iii) the transfer is of the whole claim. Those formal requirements are accepted as met here. The claim against Hayworth is a classic chose in action; it is part of the company’s property and, absent an express statutory or common‑law prohibition, is freely assignable.

Public‑policy objections do not displace a valid statutory assignment in these circumstances. Maintenance and champerty target “officious intermeddlers” trafficking in strangers’ litigation for profit. John Cameron is not a stranger: he is the former director and principal shareholder whose economic fate was directly tied to Arnext’s success. His assumption of the very substantial burden and risk of funding and conducting the litigation is lawful consideration and a legitimate commercial purpose, not improper trafficking.

The suggestion that the assignment is merely a device to evade representation rules misconceives the effect of the transfer. Once assigned, the cause of action is no longer the company’s: it vests in Mr Cameron personally. Courts have repeatedly treated such choses in action as assignable even where the practical consequence is that the assignee prosecutes litigation which the assignor could not or would not pursue. The rule that a company must be represented by a lawyer cannot be extended to prohibit the company from alienating its property in a manner expressly contemplated by statute.

Concerns about fiduciary duties and undervalue are internal company matters. Here, the board/shareholders were fully aware of Arnext’s impecuniosity and consciously opted for an assignment that preserved a chance of recovery instead of abandoning the claim. To invalidate that solution would unjustifiably restrict access to the courts for under‑resourced companies and contradict the property‑based scheme of section 28.

Section 28 of the Supreme Court of Judicature (Ireland) Act 1877 expressly permits the absolute assignment of legal choses in action, including causes of action for damages, provided the assignment is in writing and with notice to the debtor. Those formal requirements are satisfied here. Once an absolute assignment is made, the assignee sues in his own name; the claim becomes his property. The statute does not impose a “motive” test, and the courts should not read in a disqualifying purpose where the text does not.

The public‑policy objections also fail. Maintenance and champerty target officious intermeddling and trafficking in litigation by strangers. Mr. Cameron is not a stranger: he is the principal shareholder and former director whose economic interests are already aligned with Arnext. He is not speculating in others’ disputes; he is seeking to vindicate a claim that directly affects his own stake. That is the paradigm case where courts have tolerated, even expected, active pursuit of litigation.

Nor is this a disguised evasion of the rule that companies appear by lawyers. After assignment, the claim is no longer a corporate asset; it is Cameron’s personal chose in action. The representation rule, which protects the court and third parties when a corporation appears, simply has no application once the corporation is no longer a party.

Company‑law concerns about transfer for nominal consideration go, at most, to internal validity and directors’ duties, not to the external effectiveness of an otherwise proper assignment as between Arnext, Cameron, and Hayworth. If Arnext’s members or liquidator object, they have their own remedies; Hayworth cannot rely on hypothetical internal governance issues to defeat an assignee’s statutory right to sue.

Refusing to recognize this assignment would, in practice, bar an otherwise arguable €11 million claim solely because an impecunious company cannot fund lawyers, undermining access to justice and the property‑like character of legal claims that section 28 was designed to protect.

Section 28 of the 1877 Act is the starting point: it authorises the absolute assignment of legal choses in action where the assignment is in writing, signed, and notice is given. Those formal requirements are met. The claim is a classic chose in action—no different in principle from a debt or contractual right—and Irish and common‑law authority recognise such rights as freely assignable property.

Once validly assigned, the cause of action becomes John Cameron’s personal property. The “corporate representation” rules are therefore beside the point: Arnext is no longer suing; Cameron, as the legal and beneficial owner of the claim, is. Courts have repeatedly treated motive as irrelevant where the assignment is absolute and not a mere authorisation to sue in another’s name. The fact that one motive here was to enable prosecution of the claim does not vitiate a transaction that the statute expressly contemplates.

Nor is there maintenance or champerty. Cameron is not a stranger trafficking in litigation; he is the principal shareholder and former director, directly exposed to the economic consequences of Arnext’s loss. He has a genuine, substantial interest in the outcome and seeks to enforce a pre‑existing right, not to stir up speculative litigation.

On company‑law concerns, the transaction was not a clandestine stripping of assets but a means to monetise a single, contingent asset that the company was otherwise incapable of realising. Directors’ fiduciary duties are satisfied where, as here, the arrangement maximises the only realistic prospect of recovery for the company and its stakeholders. Any benefit to Cameron is aligned, not adverse, to the company’s interests.

To invalidate this assignment would, in practice, bar impecunious companies from vindicating serious commercial wrongs, undermining both the property‑nature of choses in action and fundamental access to justice.

Hayworth Automation should prevail because the purported assignment is neither a genuine transfer of property nor compatible with fundamental public‑policy and company‑law principles.

First, in substance the cause of action remains that of Arnext Controls and Engineering Limited. The alleged €11m loss was suffered by the company, not by Mr Cameron personally. The “assignment” adds nothing but a change of nominal plaintiff; the underlying commercial reality, evidence, and alleged losses are identical. That is precisely the type of device the rules on corporate representation, security for costs, and champerty are designed to prevent.

Section 28 of the 1877 Act enables legal assignments of choses in action; it does not abolish centuries‑old public‑policy limits on trafficking in litigation. Courts have consistently held that even formally compliant assignments are void if their dominant purpose is to evade restrictions on who may litigate, or to enable an under‑resourced party to wage speculative litigation without exposure to the normal procedural safeguards. Here, the assignment’s avowed function is to allow a non‑lawyer director to prosecute a corporate claim and sidestep rules requiring representation by counsel and potential security for costs. That is classic improper maintenance.

Second, the transaction offends core company‑law principles. A very substantial corporate asset—the sole significant asset of an insolvent or near‑insolvent company—has been transferred to an insider for nominal value, outside any recognized commercial context (such as a liquidator’s sale). That squarely conflicts with directors’ fiduciary duties to act in the company’s interests and to preserve corporate assets for creditors, not to siphon them to a principal shareholder to pursue personal litigation leverage.

Permitting this assignment would invite abuse: any impecunious company could strip out claims, defeat creditor protections, avoid security for costs, and have lay directors litigate in person. The court should therefore hold the assignment invalid and dismiss Mr Cameron’s claim.

Hayworth Automation should prevail because the purported assignment to Mr. Cameron is a sham transaction that offends both public policy and core principles of company law.

First, in substance the cause of action and the alleged loss remain those of Arnext Controls and Engineering Limited. The pleaded damages are corporate losses arising from the alleged exclusion of Arnext from a project. Re‑labelling that corporate chose in action as Mr. Cameron’s personal claim does not transform its nature. Section 28 of the 1877 Act facilitates the procedural enforcement of genuine assignments; it does not license the manufacture of standing to evade mandatory rules on corporate representation, security for costs, and the corporate veil.

Second, the transaction squarely raises maintenance and champerty concerns. The assignment is not part of any recognised commercial structure—no sale by a liquidator, no factoring of debt, no genuine financing arrangement. Its sole evident purpose is to enable a non‑lawyer insider to run corporate litigation in his own name, free from the controls that would otherwise apply to impecunious companies. Authorities make clear that courts must examine the circumstances of such assignments; where the “deal” is merely trafficking in litigation or a device to sidestep legal impediments, it is void on public policy grounds.

Third, as a matter of company law, a substantial asset—an €11 million claim—cannot lawfully be transferred to a director/shareholder for nominal consideration without rigorous compliance with fiduciary duties, proper valuation, and approval procedures. A disposition that strips the company of its only significant asset, for little or no value, to permit that director to litigate for his own benefit is antithetical to directors’ duties to act in the best interests of the company and its creditors.

To uphold this assignment would invite routine circumvention of corporate and procedural safeguards. The court should declare the assignment invalid and dismiss Mr. Cameron’s attempt to proceed as plaintiff.

Hayworth Automation should prevail because the purported assignment is invalid both under section 28 and on fundamental public‑policy and company‑law grounds.

First, section 28 does not operate in a vacuum; it enables legal assignments only where they are not contrary to law or public policy. The “claim” here is quintessentially that of Arnext Controls and Engineering Limited: the alleged exclusive distribution arrangement, the supposed exclusion from a Dublin project, and the €11 million loss all concern the company’s business, not John Cameron’s personal dealings. The supposed transfer does nothing to change the underlying reality that the dispute is corporate. It is therefore an attempted end‑run around mandatory rules that (i) a company must appear by qualified legal representatives, and (ii) an impecunious corporate plaintiff may be required to give security for costs.

Second, public‑policy doctrines of maintenance and champerty require courts to scrutinise the circumstances of an assignment. Authorities recognise that “trafficking in litigation” is impermissible unless embedded in a recognised commercial context (e.g., assignment by a liquidator, factoring, subrogation by insurers). Here there is no genuine commercial transaction: no arm’s‑length price, no assumption of liabilities, no independent interest by Cameron separate from the litigation itself. The only substantive “benefit” Cameron acquires is the right to litigate without the constraints that bind the company. That is champertous in substance.

Third, as a matter of company law, a substantial corporate asset—a multi‑million‑euro claim—is being transferred to an insider for nominal or no consideration. That threatens the integrity of the capital maintenance regime and conflicts with directors’ fiduciary duties to deal with company property for proper purposes and at fair value. A court should not enforce an assignment that itself rests on a breach of duty by those purporting to effect it.

To uphold this assignment would licence shareholders and directors of insolvent or asset‑poor companies to strip out claims and litigate personally, collapsing settled protections on representation, security for costs, and corporate governance. The assignment should therefore be declared invalid and the proceedings against Hayworth dismissed.

Hayworth Automation should prevail because the purported assignment is a device to evade mandatory rules on corporate litigation, contrary to section 28, public policy, and company law.

First, section 28 of the 1877 Act does not confer a free‑standing right to traffic in litigation. It only validates “absolute assignments” that are otherwise lawful. The court must therefore examine substance, not form. Here, the underlying claim, alleged loss, and true economic interest remain those of Arnext Controls and Engineering Limited. The only practical effect of the “assignment” is to permit Mr. Cameron, a non‑lawyer, to run corporate litigation in person and to sidestep security for costs. That is precisely the kind of arrangement the maintenance and champerty authorities require the court to police and refuse.

Second, valid assignments of bare causes of action are confined to recognized categories: e.g., liquidators realising assets, insurers pursuing subrogated claims, or factoring of debts. Those contexts involve genuine commercial transactions, arm’s‑length pricing, and supervision mechanisms. By contrast, this transfer is insider self‑dealing for nominal value, with no independent commercial purpose beyond litigation. To enforce it would endorse champertous “trafficking” in corporate claims and open the door to directors stripping companies of litigation assets whenever professional representation is unaffordable.

Third, company law principles independently condemn the transaction. A cause of action for €11 million is a core corporate asset. Directors’ fiduciary duties require they protect, not dispose of, such property for token consideration to themselves. An assignment that is both value‑less and control‑conferring is a breach of duty and an unlawful reduction of the company’s asset base. Courts will not lend their authority to enforce an agreement born of such breaches.

Accordingly, the assignment is invalid and unenforceable; Arnext Controls remains the only proper plaintiff, and the proceedings in Mr. Cameron’s name must fail.

Hayworth Automation should prevail because the purported assignment is a transparent device to evade fundamental rules of company and litigation law, and is therefore invalid on both statutory and public‑policy grounds.

First, section 28 of the 1877 Act does not confer a free‑standing right to traffic in bare rights to litigate. It permits assignment only of “legal choses in action” in a manner consistent with existing equitable and public‑policy limits. Irish and common‑law authority require courts to scrutinise the *substance* of an assignment to ensure it is not maintenance or champerty. Here, the “asset” is nothing but an unliquidated damages claim; there is no underlying business, debt, or commercial portfolio being transferred. That is classic trafficking in litigation, not a recognised commercial transaction such as liquidation realisation or debt factoring.

Second, the dispute and the alleged €11 million loss remain those of Arnext Controls and Engineering Limited. Cameron’s role as former director and shareholder does not alter that reality. The supposed assignment serves only to allow a non‑lawyer to prosecute what is, in substance, a corporate claim, sidestepping rules on corporate representation and potential security for costs. Arrangements whose very object is to defeat those procedural safeguards are contrary to public policy and cannot be validated by re‑labelling them “assignments.”

Third, as a matter of company law, transferring a major corporate asset to an insider for nominal or no consideration, in circumstances of financial distress, conflicts with directors’ fiduciary duties and capital‑maintenance principles. A transaction that is ultra vires or in breach of duty cannot ground a valid statutory assignment.

Finally, access‑to‑justice concerns cannot justify dismantling settled rules against champerty, improper maintenance, and abuse of the corporate form. The only coherent outcome is to hold the assignment invalid and to refuse Cameron’s substitution as plaintiff.

Section 4(3)(j) must be read according to its text, context, and purpose. The Oireachtas deliberately used the general term “public policy”, distinct from the more specific “national security”, and did so in a provision that expressly confers a broad discretion to refuse permission to land. Nothing in the Act confines “public policy” to person‑specific, security‑type threats; to read such a limitation in would rewrite the statute.

Immigration control, by its nature, operates through forward‑looking, general policies rather than only ex post responses to individual misconduct. The 2011 guidelines, lawfully issued by the Minister, long pre‑dating Covid‑19, clearly state that non‑EEA nationals will not be admitted where the intended course is wholly online or distance‑only. That policy is rationally connected to maintaining the integrity of the student immigration route, which is a classic public policy concern recognised in the 2004 Act.

The pandemic measures did not create a new or ad hoc rule; they applied an existing, published policy to a changed factual matrix in which English‑language providers had, by government direction, moved entirely online. The applicants thus fell squarely within a known category of persons whom the State had signalled might be refused entry. That is the antithesis of arbitrary decision‑making.

The applicants’ construction would render section 4(3)(j) largely redundant, collapsing it into “national security” and depriving the Executive of the flexibility needed to manage migration in the public interest. It would also conflict with well‑established principles that immigration control involves wide, though reviewable, administrative discretion exercised by reference to general policies, provided those policies are published, coherent, and applied fairly—as they were here.

Accordingly, “public policy” in s.4(3)(j) encompasses the Minister’s long‑standing policy on distance‑only study and justifies the refusals in this case.

Section 4 of the Immigration Act 2004 is framed on the premise that non‑nationals have no right of entry and that admission is a matter of executive discretion, exercised at the frontiers in real time. Within that scheme, s.4(3)(j) expressly permits refusal where admission “would be contrary to public policy,” without any textual requirement of individualised wrongdoing or national‑security‑type conduct. The Oireachtas used a deliberately broad, general term; it could easily have confined the ground to “national security” or “public order” if that narrower concept were intended.

“Public policy” in immigration law must be understood functionally: it enables the State to operate coherent, prospective rules on who will be permitted to enter at all, in furtherance of legitimate objectives such as orderly migration control and, here, pandemic management. That necessarily includes rules framed by category rather than by individual fault. The 2011 guidelines, published and consistently applied, do exactly this: they specify that entry will not be granted for purely distance/online English‑language courses. In late 2020 that policy dovetailed with public‑health imperatives and clear public warnings not to travel for courses then being delivered remotely.

The respondents were thus on explicit notice that entry might be refused; they fall squarely within a stable, decade‑long policy which is rationally connected to maintaining integrity of the student‑immigration route and, at the relevant time, to minimising unnecessary inbound travel. Nothing in the Act or its history suggests that “public policy” is confined to case‑by‑case assessments of dangerousness. To read in such a limitation would defeat the evident legislative purpose of equipping border officials to give effect to general, prospective policies.

Accordingly, the Minister acted within the statutory power in refusing permission to land, and the challenges must fail.

Section 4(3)(j) must be read in its statutory and practical context. The Immigration Act 2004 expressly confers a broad, discretionary power to control entry “in the interests of public policy.” The phrase is not qualified by any requirement of prior misconduct or specific, individualised threat, unlike neighbouring grounds that explicitly target particular behaviours (e.g. criminality, security). The deliberate contrast indicates that “public policy” is a wider, forward-looking ground that may be implemented through general rules.

Immigration control is inherently systemic. It cannot sensibly be confined to reactive, case‑by‑case judgments about proven dangers. The Oireachtas chose an open-textured concept precisely to allow the Executive to adopt and apply overarching policies that protect societal interests: here, maintaining an orderly immigration system during a public health emergency and preventing the circumvention of long‑standing limits on distance‑only study.

The 2011 guidelines, predating Covid‑19, lawfully articulated a policy that non‑EEA students would not be admitted where the course exists only online. That policy is rationally connected to the statutory aim of ensuring that student permission is reserved for genuine, in‑person educational engagement, not as a proxy route to residence. The pandemic did not invalidate that objective; government directives moving teaching online simply meant that, for a period, the substantive condition of in‑person study was not met. The applicants were expressly warned of this.

“Public policy” in s.4(3)(j) comfortably encompasses the application of such a published, consistently applied entry rule. Requiring proof that each individual poses a grave, security‑type threat would collapse s.4(3)(j) into the separate “security” ground and emasculate the legislature’s chosen language. On a faithful, purposive reading, the Minister acted within the broad discretion conferred by the Act, and the refusals of permission to land were lawful.

Section 4(3)(j) must be read according to its text, context and purpose. The Oireachtas chose an open‑textured ground – “contrary to public policy” – in a provision explicitly conferring a power to refuse “permission to land” at the border. That phrase is not qualified by any requirement of individual misconduct, nor is it limited to national‑security type threats; if such a limitation were intended, the legislature could and would have said so expressly, as it has done in other statutes.

Border control is, by its nature, a domain of prospective, category‑based judgment. The Act’s purpose is to confer a practical mechanism to manage who may enter Ireland in the interests of societal wellbeing. “Public policy” here therefore reasonably embraces coherent, published policies directed to systemic objectives—such as avoiding the use of the student route to facilitate de facto migration for distance‑only courses, and, in 2020, managing serious public‑health and system‑capacity pressures.

The Minister’s 2011 guidelines pre‑dated Covid‑19 and have consistently stated that non‑EEA nationals will not be admitted where the proposed course is distance/online only. In 2020, this was reiterated and expressly notified to prospective English‑language students. The applicants chose to travel knowing, or being fixed with knowledge, that only online tuition was then available and that admission might be refused.

Far from being arbitrary, the policy is rational, transparent, and directly connected to legitimate State goals: maintaining the integrity and orderly operation of the student immigration route and, in the pandemic context, minimising non‑essential arrivals. Applying that long‑standing, public policy to these facts is a paradigmatic exercise of the wide discretion the 2004 Act entrusts to immigration officers.

Accordingly, “public policy” in s.4(3)(j) encompasses the Minister’s published entry policies, and the refusals of permission to land were lawful.

Section 4(3)(j) must be read in its own statutory setting. The Immigration Act 2004 is a framework for prospective, ex ante control of admission, not retrospective punishment for wrongdoing. Within that framework, s.4 confers a broad discretion on the immigration officer to decide, at the point of entry, whether admission would be “contrary to … public policy.” Nothing in the text limits that phrase to cases of identified, individual misconduct or national security in the narrow sense. Had the Oireachtas wished to confine it so, it could have done so expressly, as it did in adjacent provisions addressing security and public order.

“Public policy” in immigration law has always included the State’s legitimate objectives in managing who may enter and on what terms. That necessarily embraces general, forward‑looking policies—particularly where they are (i) published, (ii) long‑standing, and (iii) rationally connected to the statutory purpose of controlled and orderly entry. The 2011 guidelines squarely stated that non‑EEA students would not be admitted for purely online or distance courses. In 2020, with Covid‑19 restrictions in place, that policy directly applied: the only form of the proposed study was remote. Admission in such circumstances would undermine the coherent administration of the student immigration regime and, in the pandemic context, the State’s public‑health strategy. Preventing that outcome is a quintessential matter of “public policy.”

The applicants do not challenge the legality of the guidelines themselves; they instead seek to rewrite s.4(3)(j) so that it cannot operate by reference to any general policy. That construction is incompatible with the text, with the evident legislative aim of giving flexible tools for border control, and with practical necessity: immigration officers cannot be required to identify personal misconduct before applying a rule that a defined category of entrants (here, online‑only students) will not be admitted. Properly construed, “public policy” includes the Minister’s published policy, and the refusals were lawful.

Section 4(3)(j) must be read in light of constitutional limits on executive power, the structure of the 2004 Act, and cognate uses of “public policy” in Irish and EU law. Properly construed, “public policy” is an exceptional ground, reserved for genuine, serious threats to the State’s core interests, not a catch‑all for implementing general immigration preferences.

First, the “public policy or security” formulation links two grave concepts. The canon of noscitur a sociis requires “public policy” to be read ejusdem generis with “security” concerns—i.e. situations involving tangible risks posed by particular individuals. A mere disagreement with the mode of tuition of an otherwise lawful course is qualitatively different.

Second, the Minister already has very broad, explicit powers elsewhere in the Act to control entry on ordinary administrative grounds (e.g. financial means, visas, documentation). To treat s.4(3)(j) as an open‑ended power to operationalise any forward‑looking policy would render those more specific provisions largely redundant and subvert the Oireachtas’ evident choice to confine exceptional refusal to narrower, high‑threshold cases.

Third, legislative history and comparative materials show that where the Oireachtas intends broad programmatic discretion, it says so; when it uses “public policy” in tandem with “security,” it signals a need for an individualised, conduct‑based assessment. Here, there was no allegation that either applicant posed any public health, security, or societal risk; they were compliant students intending to follow State‑mandated online teaching.

Fourth, guidelines cannot expand a statutory ground of refusal beyond its proper meaning. A Ministerial policy against distance‑learning migrants, even if longstanding, cannot convert a non‑threat into a “public policy” danger.

Accordingly, the refusals—resting solely on a generalized, non‑individualized policy about online courses—fell outside s.4(3)(j). The court should quash the decisions and restrain the applicants’ removal.

Section 4(3)(j) must be interpreted in light of its text, structure, and constitutional context. Properly construed, “public policy” in this provision is not a roving mandate to enforce any general governmental preference at the border, but a tightly confined ground akin to national security or serious threats to fundamental societal interests.

First, “public policy” appears in a list of grave exclusion grounds (security of the State, public safety, public health). Applying noscitur a sociis, its meaning must be read ejusdem generis with these: it targets concrete, serious risks, not routine regulatory objectives such as managing the mode of teaching on a private language course.

Second, Irish and EU usages of “public policy” in migration and free‑movement contexts consistently link it to individual conduct posing a genuine, sufficiently serious threat. The Minister’s broad construction—allowing exclusion of any compliant traveler because they do not fit a policy preference—collides with that settled understanding and turns an exceptional power into a general gatekeeping tool.

Third, the Oireachtas has historically resisted open‑ended executive discretions in immigration law. To allow published guidelines on online courses to be laundered through the “public policy” ground is to delegate to the Minister the very power the legislature chose not to grant expressly: a categorical bar on distance‑learning students.

Finally, Zhao and Park are concededly law‑abiding students; no allegation of deception, health risk, or security concern is made. Denying entry solely because the pandemic temporarily shifted classes online is divorced from their personal conduct and from any real threat to the State’s core interests. On a correct, narrower reading of s.4(3)(j), the refusals were ultra vires and must be quashed.

Section 4(3)(j) must be construed in light of constitutional norms, legislative history, and cognate uses of “public policy” in Irish and EU law. So viewed, “public policy” is an exceptional ground, reserved for protecting fundamental interests of society from conduct that is actually or potentially harmful, not a catch‑all enabling the executive to refuse entry whenever it wishes to advance general policy goals.

First, the 2004 Act already confers broad discretion via multiple, more specific grounds for refusal. Interpreting “public policy” as an open‑ended warrant for general immigration management would render those other grounds largely superfluous and defeat the Oireachtas’ evident intention to cabin executive power rather than recreate, via a vague phrase, a general, unreviewable discretion.

Second, both domestic and international materials treat “public policy” (and the closely associated “public security”) as tied to threats to essential State interests, normally linked to the individual’s conduct or characteristics—crime, disorder, national security—not to the mere fact that a person wishes to pursue an online course. There is no suggestion that Zhao or Park pose any such threat; they are ordinary students who complied with published requirements and travelled openly.

Third, the Minister’s reliance on the 2011 guidelines and pandemic‑era circulars is misplaced. Those are policy instruments, not legislation. They cannot lawfully expand “public policy” in s.4(3)(j) to include a purely administrative preference that language courses be face‑to‑face. To allow general guidance to define the scope of a statutory ground of refusal would invert the hierarchy of norms and undermine legal certainty.

Finally, proportionality and fair procedures demand individualised assessment. Denial of entry grounded solely on a generic, distance‑learning policy—wholly untethered to any personal wrongdoing or risk—falls outside the proper, narrow meaning of “public policy” and is therefore ultra vires.

Section 4(3)(j) must be read in light of the structure, history, and constitutional setting of Irish immigration law. Properly construed, “public policy” here cannot mean any generally announced executive preference about who should enter, but is confined to situations where an individual’s presence poses a genuine, particularised threat to fundamental interests of the State.

First, the phrase “public policy or … security” appears as a paired limitation on the Minister’s power. Security plainly concerns serious threats; “public policy” must be interpreted ejusdem generis, covering similarly weighty, concrete risks, not routine administrative tidiness. Otherwise, the limiting words do no real work, and the Minister gains an unfettered, standardless veto over entry.

Second, comparative domestic and international usage has consistently confined “public policy” in migration contexts to serious threats to public order or core societal interests, grounded in the conduct or circumstances of the individual non‑national. The Oireachtas, aware of such usage and of the dangers of broad Henry VIII‑style clauses, chose not to enact a free‑standing power to enforce all executive “policies” at the border; it chose the narrower term.

Third, the Minister’s own 2011 guidelines confirm that a separate, specific policy instrument is required when refusing non‑EEA students whose courses are online. Resort to section 4(3)(j) here attempts to collapse that distinct, policy‑based regime into a generic “public policy” ground, sidestepping the need for a lawful, proportionate, and individualized assessment.

Charlie Zhao and Alex Park presented no individual risk whatever: they are bona fide students, complying with published entry conditions, whose courses moved online only because of State‑mandated pandemic measures. Denying admission solely because their classes are remote is not the protection of “public policy” in the statutory sense; it is the impermissible use of a narrow, exceptional ground as a broad policy catch‑all. Their refusals were therefore ultra vires and should be quashed.

Section 4(3)(j) must be read narrowly if it is not to become a carte blanche for exclusion on any policy ground the Executive might later identify. The phrase “public policy” appears in a list alongside threats to “national security” and other grave interests, signalling through noscitur a sociis that it is aimed at serious, concrete risks, not general administrative preferences.

Irish and comparative materials show “public policy” as an exceptional ground, invoked to protect core State interests against identifiable harm. It is not a synonym for “any policy the Minister may wish to pursue.” To accept the Minister’s construction would collapse the carefully delimited statutory grounds into a general discretion inconsistent with the Oireachtas’s evident concern—reflected in the 2004 Act’s structure—to avoid open‑ended power and to require specific statutory justification for exclusion.

On the facts, there is no allegation that either Mr Zhao or Mr Park posed any individual risk to security, public health, or public order. Their sole “failing” is that, because of a temporary pandemic measure, their chosen courses were delivered online. The 2011 guidelines, even if validly made, cannot enlarge the statutory term “public policy” so as to convert a non‑threatening, fully lawful intention to study into a basis for exclusion. Guidelines must conform to the statute, not rewrite it.

Moreover, a construction allowing exclusion whenever the Executive articulates a forward‑looking “strategy” would undermine legal certainty for all migrants, particularly students who planned their travel on the basis of published schemes. It would permit de facto law‑making by circular under the guise of “public policy.”

Properly interpreted, s.4(3)(j) is not engaged on these facts. The refusals were ultra vires, and Mr Zhao and Mr Park are entitled to relief preventing their removal.

Greenfields Mortgage Corporation PLC should prevail because, even assuming Alan Fitzgerald never validly contracted, he was unjustly enriched at the bank’s expense and cannot invoke the Consumer Credit Act 1995 to retain a windfall produced by forgery.

First, the bank advanced substantial funds under a clear mistake: it reasonably believed Alan had signed, was a co‑borrower, and that it held a valid security over the family home. That belief was induced by documentation that on its face bore his signature and marital confirmation. This satisfies the core elements of restitution for mistaken payment.

Second, enrichment is clear. The 2003 and 2007 advances were paid into the Fitzgeralds’ joint account, the vehicle for the household’s entire financial life. From there they funded tax clearances, a pension contribution with long‑term benefits, acquisition of a field and, significantly, discharge of the 2003 loan itself. Alan’s income was routinely commingled with these loan proceeds; he and his family enjoyed the use and advantages of the funds. Under well‑established authority, use of misdirected money to meet joint liabilities and acquire family assets constitutes a recoverable enrichment, even where the recipient did not personally arrange the borrowing.

Third, the Consumer Credit Act 1995 does not immunise a non‑signatory who denies any contract. The Act regulates enforceability of “agreements” and the duties of creditors to contracting consumers. If Alan’s signature was forged, there is no “agreement” with him to which the Act can attach; it cannot be repurposed as a shield to defeat restitution for money paid under a fundamental mistake. Case law confirms that the existence (or invalidity) of a contract with someone else does not bar restitutionary claims against a distinct, enriched beneficiary.

Finally, any “change of position” defence fails: Alan has not shown specific, irreversible reliance on the mistaken payments distinct from ordinary household spending. Equity should require him to restore, at least, the measurable benefits received.

Greenfields is entitled to succeed, at least in substantial restitution, even if Alan Fitzgerald’s signature was forged and no enforceable credit contract ever arose.

First, the bank advanced €40,000 in 2003 and €200,000 in 2007 under a clear mistake of fact: it believed Alan had signed, consented, and that it held security over the jointly owned home. That is the paradigm case for restitution for payments made under mistake. The fact that the immediate contract was with Elaine, or void as against Alan, does not bar recovery from a third party who was in fact enriched: established authority permits a restitutionary claim against a non‑contracting beneficiary.

Second, enrichment and its connection to the mistaken loans are clear. The 2007 funds were paid into the joint account through which the family’s entire financial life was run. From there, they were applied to pay tax liabilities, fund a pension, acquire a field, and discharge the 2003 loan secured on the jointly owned home. Those are direct economic benefits to Alan: reduced personal and household liabilities and acquisition/improvement of family assets. His own fishing income does not negate that benefit; the scale and timing of the inflows and applications strongly support tracing to the loan funds.

Third, the Consumer Credit Act 1995 regulates the enforceability of credit agreements; it does not confer an immunity to restitution when a consumer denies ever having contracted. To hold otherwise would convert statutory protection into a licence to keep money obtained by forgery. Nor is there any pleaded “change of position” of a kind that would make restitution inequitable—Alan simply lived in a household whose debts were paid down and assets enhanced.

Equity and principle therefore require that Alan make restitution to Greenfields, to the extent of the benefits he received, which on the evidence approaches the full sums advanced.

Alan Fitzgerald should be held liable in restitution, even if no valid contractual mortgage existed in his name.

First, there is clear enrichment. The 2007 loan proceeds were paid into the Fitzgeralds’ *joint* current account, the very vehicle used for the family’s general finances and funded by Alan’s fishing income. From that account, the funds discharged tax liabilities, paid a Department of Family and Social Affairs pension contribution, and financed the purchase of a field, as well as clearing the earlier 2003 loan. These are quintessential family and asset-building expenditures. Even if Elaine orchestrated the borrowing, Alan’s household and assets were substantially improved.

Second, the enrichment was at Greenfields’ expense and arose from a clear mistake: the bank advanced funds on the faith of what appeared to be Alan’s signatures and a valid charge over the jointly owned home. But for that mistaken belief, it would not have advanced the loans or released them into the joint account.

Third, no sufficient “change of position” defense arises. The expenditures were voluntary applications of money for family and property purposes, not irreversible detrimental reliance induced by Greenfields. Equity does not entitle Alan to retain benefits simply because they have been spent, particularly where they improved his family’s position and cleared his household liabilities.

Fourth, the Consumer Credit Act 1995 does not immunize a non-signing spouse from restitutionary liability. The Act regulates enforceability of *credit agreements*; it does not purport to abolish the long‑standing law of unjust enrichment where money is paid under a fundamental mistake or fraud. To hold otherwise would weaponize consumer protection legislation as a shield for retaining mistakenly advanced funds.

Finally, established authority permits restitution against a non-contracting beneficiary even where the bank also has (or believed it had) contractual rights against another. The proper outcome is a restitutionary order requiring Alan Fitzgerald to repay the value of the benefits received.

Alan Fitzgerald cannot both disavow the loan contracts and retain the substantial benefits they financed. Even assuming his signature was forged and no contract exists, Greenfields is entitled to restitution.

First, the bank advanced large sums under a clear mistake: it reasonably believed Alan had signed and that it held security over the jointly owned home. That mistake directly induced the advances. The proceeds were then paid into the spouses’ joint account, the very vehicle by which the household—and thus Alan—conducted its finances. From that commingled fund, the money was applied to quintessentially joint or family purposes: tax liabilities, a pension contribution, discharge of the 2003 loan nominally in his name, and acquisition of a field adjacent to the family home. These are not purely personal indulgences of Elaine; they objectively enhanced the couple’s financial position and relieved liabilities that otherwise would have fallen on Alan.

Restitution does not require a contract; it requires enrichment at the plaintiff’s expense, causation, and absence of a defence. All are present. The existence of a contractual claim against Elaine does not preclude a concurrent restitutionary claim against Alan as a distinct recipient of the mistaken benefit.

The Consumer Credit Act 1995 regulates enforceability of credit agreements; it does not confer a licence to retain money obtained under forgery. To hold otherwise would weaponise protective legislation as a shield for unjust enrichment and incentivise abuse through forged signatures.

Nor is there a credible “change of position” defence: using mistakenly obtained funds for ordinary living and wealth-enhancing purposes, without any demonstrable detrimental reliance, cannot bar restitution. Equity demands that Alan restore at least the value of the benefits he received, and on these facts that encompasses the effective whole of the advances.

Alan Fitzgerald cannot simultaneously deny contractual liability and retain the substantial benefits advanced on the faith of his purported signature. Even if the court finds no valid contract with him because of forgery, Greenfields is still entitled to restitution in unjust enrichment.

First, enrichment is clear. The 2003 and 2007 advances were paid into the Fitzgeralds’ joint account, the common vehicle for the household’s finances. Those funds were then applied to core obligations of that household: tax liabilities, a pension contribution to the Department of Family and Social Affairs, and the purchase of a field adjacent to the family home, while also discharging the 2003 loan. These are not remote or incidental benefits; they directly improved the family’s net position and thereby Alan’s position as joint owner and account‑holder.

Second, the enrichment was at Greenfields’ expense and mistaken. The bank advanced large sums in the honest but erroneous belief that Alan had signed, and that it held effective security over the home. That is precisely the type of operative mistake long recognised as giving rise to restitution, especially where a forged instrument has induced the advance.

Third, no defence bars recovery. Alan’s “change of position” argument is weak: ordinary spending and failure to scrutinise unusually large inflows into a joint account do not amount to a protected, good‑faith reliance that would make repayment inequitable. If anything, his ongoing use of the account makes it more, not less, just that he restore funds misdirected on his behalf.

Finally, the Consumer Credit Act 1995 should not be distorted into a charter for windfalls. Those statutory protections regulate enforceability of credit agreements; they do not immunise a non‑contracting beneficiary from having to restore mistaken payments. Established authority confirms that the existence or invalidity of a contract with another party does not preclude direct restitutionary recovery from an enriched third party.

Accordingly, Greenfields should prevail in its unjust enrichment claim against Alan Fitzgerald.

Alan Fitzgerald should not be held liable, either in contract or restitution.

First, no contract ever bound him. His alleged signatures were forgeries. Under the Consumer Credit Act 1995, enforceability of regulated credit depends on strict compliance with statutory formalities and genuine borrower consent. Permitting Greenfields to recover from a non‑signing, non‑consenting spouse would nullify the Act’s protections: the lender, having chosen to rely on documents later shown to be forged, cannot re‑characterise its failed, non‑compliant credit agreement as a restitution claim to escape the statutory regime.

Second, unjust enrichment is not made out. Any “enrichment” to Alan is neither direct nor incontrovertible. The funds went into a joint account already funded by his own fishing income, then were largely applied to Elaine’s purposes: tax liabilities, pension payments, a field, and a foreign holiday home; the 2007 advance also repaid the 2003 loan, which he likewise never authorised. Commingling in a joint account destroys the bank’s ability to trace specific benefits to Alan personally, especially where he was frequently away and entrusted day‑to‑day finances to his spouse. At most, any incidental benefit is diffuse and unquantified, far from justifying liability for the full €240,000.

Third, even if enrichment were shown, powerful defenses apply. Alan reasonably relied on the appearance that household finances stemmed from his own earnings and ordinary, smaller‑scale arrangements by Elaine. Had he been put on proper notice that large, secured loans were taken out in his name, he could have intervened early, refused consent, or restructured affairs. Requiring full repayment now would impose on an innocent spouse the loss properly borne by the professional lender that failed to verify his consent.

Both contract and restitution routes are therefore barred; judgment should be for Alan Fitzgerald.

Alan Fitzgerald should not be held liable, either in contract or in restitution.

First, there is no contract. A forged signature is a nullity; it cannot create contractual obligations. Greenfields chose to advance consumer credit on the assumption of a joint loan, secured on jointly owned property. The Consumer Credit Act 1995 conditions enforceability on strict compliance with formality and disclosure requirements vis‑à‑vis the borrower. As against Alan, there was never a compliant agreement at all. Allowing the bank to re‑label its claim as “restitution” would defeat the Act’s protective purpose by imposing liability on a consumer whom the statute treats as not having validly contracted.

Second, unjust enrichment is not made out. Any “enrichment” is speculative and unquantified. The funds passed into a joint current account into which Alan continuously paid his own earnings. They were then dispersed to varied purposes, some plainly Elaine’s (tax, pension, prior loan, a field; no investment property was ever built). The bank cannot reliably trace what, if anything, was Alan’s net benefit as distinct from his spouse’s or the ordinary use of his own income. Restitution cannot be awarded on conjecture.

Third, even if some benefit were shown, powerful change‑of‑position and fairness defenses apply. Alan was frequently away fishing, reasonably trusted his spouse with day‑to‑day finances, and had no reason to suspect a large, forged loan. Had he been properly informed—as he would have been under a compliant joint lending process—he could have refused consent or intervened early. The entire loss flows from the bank’s unilateral error and its failure to verify his signature and independent consent, not from any fault of his.

The risk of forgery and non‑compliance with consumer credit rules must rest with the sophisticated lender that failed to protect itself, not with an unwitting spouse.

Alan Fitzgerald cannot be made liable in contract or in restitution.

First, on the facts as accepted for this exercise, his signature was forged. A forged signature is a nullity: no consensus ad idem, no contract, no mortgage. The Consumer Credit Act 1995 is premised on written, properly executed consumer credit agreements. Where a lender advances funds on the strength of a forged co‑borrower signature, it has failed to obtain a valid agreement from that person. It would invert the Act’s protective purpose to allow a lender, having omitted to ensure genuine consent and statutory compliance, to bypass those requirements via restitution.

Second, public policy is clear: statutory consumer safeguards cannot be sidestepped by re‑characterising an unenforceable or non‑existent loan as an unjust enrichment claim. To permit recovery in such circumstances would weaken the Act’s protections for vulnerable spouses – the very situation here, where one spouse manages finances and the other is often away and reliant on trust.

Third, Greenfields cannot prove a specific, net enrichment of Alan attributable to the loans. His own fishing income was regularly deposited into the same joint account, and the 2007 funds were largely used for Elaine’s purposes (tax, pension, a field, clearing the 2003 loan). No investment property was built; no clear, enduring asset is traceable to him. At most, any incidental household benefit is indistinguishable from what his own earnings would have funded. That uncertainty defeats the bank’s burden to show quantifiable enrichment.

Finally, Alan has a powerful change‑of‑position defence: had he been alerted that large borrowings were being run through the account in his name, he could have frozen the account, confronted the forgery, or restructured family finances. Holding him liable now would be both legally unsound and substantively unfair.

Alan Fitzgerald cannot be held liable in contract or restitution.

First, there is no valid contract. On Alan’s uncontested evidence, his signature on the 2003 and 2007 loan and mortgage documents was forged. A forged “signature” is a nullity: no agreement, no consent, no security. Under the Consumer Credit Act 1995, Greenfields was obliged to ensure proper execution, disclosure and warnings in respect of a consumer borrower. Those protections are meaningless if a lender, having failed even to verify a basic signature and marital consent, can bypass the Act by re‑characterising its claim as “restitution”.

Second, public policy and precedent reject using unjust enrichment to defeat a specific consumer‑credit regime. The Oireachtas deliberately placed the risk of defective documentation and inadequate verification on regulated lenders, not unsuspecting spouses who never signed. Allowing recovery here would invite lenders to relax statutory compliance, confident they can always fall back on restitution.

Third, Greenfields has not shown a concrete enrichment of Alan personally, still less one “at the expense” of the bank. Funds were paid into a long‑standing joint account into which Alan was continuously lodging his own substantial earnings. The bank cannot trace what part of any outgoing reflected loan monies rather than his income. Joint household spending, tax payments, or paying off Elaine’s earlier debt are not demonstrably Alan’s net gain.

Finally, any putative enrichment has been irreversibly spent in the ordinary course of family life. Alan’s position has fundamentally changed; to make him repay €240,000 now is to impose on him the full loss caused by the bank’s own mistake and Elaine’s wrongdoing. Restitution is equitable; it should not be used punitively.

The claim against Alan should therefore be dismissed.

Alan Fitzgerald should not be held liable, either in contract or in restitution.

First, on the facts, there was no consensus ad idem between Alan and Greenfields. His signature was forged; he neither applied for, nor signed, nor knew of the 2003 or 2007 loans in the amounts advanced. A forged signature is a nullity. Without an actual agreement, there is no “borrower” in law and no contractual nexus on which Greenfields can sue Alan. Any purported charge over the jointly owned home, insofar as it depends on his forged signature, is likewise void.

Second, Parliament enacted the Consumer Credit Act 1995 to regulate and restrain lending to consumers and to prescribe formal requirements that go to enforceability. Allowing Greenfields to bypass those protections through restitution would subvert the legislative scheme: lenders could ignore or be careless about statutory safeguards, then fall back on unjust enrichment when things went wrong. Established authority holds that restitution cannot be used to undermine express consumer-protection policy.

Third, Greenfields cannot meet the elements of unjust enrichment against Alan. It cannot establish that he, as distinct from Elaine, was enriched in a quantifiable way. The 2007 proceeds were commingled in a joint account into which Alan was already paying substantial earnings; they were used largely for Elaine’s purposes (tax clearance, pension fund, field purchase, repayment of the earlier loan). The bank cannot reliably trace its money into any enduring asset in Alan’s hands. At most, any incidental benefit to the household is diffuse, indirect, and unmeasurable.

Finally, Alan has a robust “change of position” defence: had he been informed or had genuine notice, he could have prevented or mitigated the dissipation of funds. To impose liability for the full advance would be disproportionate and contrary to both fairness and the Act’s protective intent.

The Court should hold that the Director may rely on the communication records.

First, at the material time the Communications (Retention of Data) Act 2011 was validly enacted, presumptively constitutional legislation. Gardaí acted squarely within its terms. Under well‑settled principles, individuals are entitled—and required—to rely on statutes as they stand. Subsequent CJEU clarification of EU law cannot retrospectively convert lawful investigative steps into unlawful conduct, still less into “conscious and deliberate” breaches that would justify exclusion under domestic rules on evidence.

Second, EU law does not itself establish an automatic exclusionary rule. The CJEU decisions invoked scrutinise the compatibility of general retention regimes with the Charter, but leave questions of evidential admissibility to national procedural autonomy, subject to effectiveness and equivalence. Admitting this evidence, obtained in good faith under primary legislation, does not render EU rights ineffective: those rights are now vindicated prospectively through legislative amendment and future compliance.

Third, the intrusion here is limited and proportionate. Only traffic and location data were accessed; no content was intercepted. The data concerned a narrow temporal and geographic window directly related to a grave firearms offence. The Court can be satisfied that, had an independent prior‑authorisation regime existed, these precise measures would plainly have met any such test.

Fourth, exclusion would gravely impair the administration of justice in serious crime. The phone logs are a critical, objective means of linking the burned‑out Lexus and convoy movements to Ronan Doyle. Where investigators have acted in good faith reliance on statute, the balance between privacy and public safety favours admission, with any rights breach recognised but remedied without invalidating a properly conducted prosecution.

Accordingly, the communication records are lawfully admissible and the DPP should prevail.

The communication records are admissible and the conviction should stand.

First, at the material time the Communications (Retention of Data) Act 2011 was in full force, presumptively constitutional and binding on Gardaí. Public authorities are entitled—indeed obliged—to apply statutes as enacted unless and until they are struck down or disapplied. To retrospectively penalise the prosecution for relying in good faith on then‑valid law would undermine legal certainty and the orderly administration of justice.

Second, even measured against the standards elaborated subsequently in CJEU case law, the interference here was narrowly focused and proportionate. The data accessed concerned limited time windows, specific devices (the “001” and “002” phones) and a grave, life‑threatening firearms offence. There was no interception of content; only metadata was obtained, and solely to test whether movement and contact patterns matched the Lexus’s journey and its destruction. On any fair view, that is targeted use of retained data in pursuit of a compelling objective: detection and prosecution of serious violent crime.

Third, EU law does not require automatic exclusion of evidence obtained under a regime later found incompatible with the Charter. The Court of Justice has expressly left rules of evidence and consequences of illegality to national courts, subject to effectiveness and equivalence. Those principles are satisfied where, as here, there is (a) good‑faith reliance on legislation, (b) no deliberate or flagrant rights violation, and (c) a powerful public interest in adjudicating serious offences on their true merits.

Finally, the defendant’s privacy interests are adequately vindicated by prospective legislative reform and potential civil or constitutional remedies. They do not justify suppressing highly probative, lawfully‑obtained evidence and impeding accountability for a violent shooting.

The communication records are admissible and the conviction should stand.

First, at the time of the investigation the Communications (Retention of Data) Act 2011 was validly enacted, presumptively constitutional legislation. Gardaí were not acting on a personal frolic but in good‑faith reliance on a statute passed by the Oireachtas and in force. Fundamental principles of legal certainty and the rule of law preclude retrospectively criminalising or invalidating investigative conduct that complied with the law as it then stood, absent egregious bad faith or abuse.

Second, the CJEU’s subsequent jurisprudence (Digital Rights Ireland and progeny) addressed Member States’ legislative frameworks; it did not purport to require automatic exclusion of all evidence gathered under earlier, good‑faith regimes. The proper domestic response is to align future retention and access regimes with EU standards, not to erase past investigations of serious gun crime. To do otherwise would effectively confer de facto immunity on offenders because of later legal developments.

Third, the interference with privacy here was limited and proportionate. Only traffic and location metadata were accessed, in a time‑ and place‑bounded way, for the investigation of a grave firearms offence. No content of communications was intercepted. This is far removed from indiscriminate surveillance. On any realistic view, such access would have been authorised by an independent body had such a mechanism existed.

Fourth, exclusion is a discretionary remedy in our law, reserved for deliberate or conscious violation of rights or patently unfair prejudice. There is no such misconduct here. The accused’s trial remained fair: the records are objectively reliable; they are one strand among other evidence linking the Lexus, phones and movements to the crime.

Balancing the public interest in prosecuting serious violence against a technical, subsequently identified defect in the statutory regime, the court should admit the records and uphold the prosecution.

The Court should hold that the communications records are admissible and that the Director may rely upon them.

First, at the material time the Communications (Retention of Data) Act 2011 was validly enacted, enjoyed the presumption of constitutionality and directly empowered An Garda Síochána to seek this data. Public authorities are entitled—indeed bound—to act on the basis of legislation in force. Subject to effectiveness and equivalence, the design of evidential consequences remains for national law. Irish law has never recognised a rigid “fruit of the poisonous tree” doctrine; rather, it applies a flexible, proportionality‑based exclusionary rule focused on deliberate or conscious breach. Fourth, the public interest in prosecuting a serious shooting is compelling. To exclude highly probative, lawfully‑obtained evidence would unjustifiably undermine the administration of justice and confer an unwarranted windfall on an accused, without meaningfully advancing privacy protection.

On a proper application of national and EU law, the records are admissible and the Director should prevail.

The communication records are admissible and the conviction should stand.

First, at the material time the Communications (Retention of Data) Act 2011 was a presumptively constitutional statute, enacted by the Oireachtas and applied uniformly. Investigators were not acting in knowing defiance of EU law but in good‑faith reliance on a domestic legal framework expressly designed for serious crime. The Court has repeatedly left admissibility to Member States, subject to the principles of equivalence and effectiveness. Those principles are satisfied here: Ireland has amended its regime going forward; exclusion in this historic case is not required to vindicate EU rights or deter ongoing systemic breaches.

Third, even applying EU‑level privacy standards, the interference here is limited and proportionate. Only traffic and location data—not content—were accessed; the scope was narrow in time, geography, and persons; and the offence was extremely grave, involving a shooting with potentially lethal intent.
